13109.e: Thousands of workers and craftsmen built the pyramids. They lived in villages nearby and were paid in food.
13109.m: Thousands of Egyptian workers built the pyramids.

13110.q: How did the workers move the heavy stone blocks?
13110.e: The stones were pulled on wooden sledges and carried on boats across the Nile. Many workers pulled on ropes together.
13110.m: The stones were pulled on wooden sledges.

13111.q: What did the pyramid of the pharaoh Djoser, one of the oldest pyramids, look like?
13111.e: The Pyramid of Djoser looks like a staircase with six steps. Pyramids with smooth sides were only built later.
13111.m: The Pyramid of Djoser is a step pyramid.

13112.q: What were the Pyramids of Giza once covered with on the outside?
13112.e: A layer of pale, smooth limestone made the pyramids shine in the sun. Later these stones were taken away for other buildings.
13112.m: The pyramids once gleamed with smooth white stones.

13113.e: The pharaoh's coffin stood in the burial chamber. Passages led there from outside.
13113.m: Inside a pyramid was the burial chamber.

13114.q: What does the Great Sphinx near the Pyramids of Giza look like?
a: A lion's body with a human head
A horse's body with a bird's head
A human body with a cat's head
A snake's body with a lion's head
13114.e: The Sphinx lies like a lion and has the face of a pharaoh. It was carved out of the rock.
13114.m: The Sphinx has a lion's body and a human head.

13115.e: The Egyptians dried the bodies of the dead. This way they lasted a very long time.
13115.m: A mummy is a dead person whose body has been preserved.

13116.q: Why did the ancient Egyptians turn the dead into mummies?
a: Because the tombs were too small
13116.e: The Egyptians believed that the soul still needed the body in the afterlife. So the body was not supposed to decay.
13116.m: Mummies were meant to give the dead a life after death.

13117.q: What was a mummy wrapped in?
13117.e: Many metres of linen strips were wound around the body. Small protective amulets were often placed between them.
13117.m: Mummies were wrapped in linen bandages.

13118.q: What was used to dry the body of a mummy?
13118.e: The salt is called natron and is found in Egypt. It drew the water out of the body.
13118.m: A salt was used to dry the body.

13119.q: Which organ did the Egyptians usually leave inside the mummy's body?
13119.e: The heart was seen as the seat of thought and feeling. It was weighed in the afterlife and so had to stay in the body.
13119.m: The heart stayed in the mummy because it was needed in the afterlife.

13120.q: What were the removed organs kept in?
13120.e: These jars are called canopic jars. Their lids often had the heads of protective gods.
13120.m: The organs went into special jars, the canopic jars.

13121.q: Roughly how long did it take to make a mummy?
13121.e: Drying the body alone took many weeks. After that the body was anointed and wrapped.

13122.q: What is a large stone coffin that a mummy was placed in called?
13122.e: A sarcophagus is a coffin made of stone. It often held further wooden coffins inside.
13122.m: A large stone coffin is called a sarcophagus.

13123.q: Which god with a jackal's head protected the dead and the mummies?
13123.e: Anubis was the god of embalming. He watched over the tombs and the dead.
13123.m: Anubis with the jackal's head protected the dead.

13124.q: Were animals also mummified in ancient Egypt?
13124.e: Over a million animal mummies have been found, for example cats, birds and crocodiles. Many were gifts to the gods.
13124.m: Animals such as cats were also mummified.

13125.q: What did the Egyptians place in the tomb with the dead?
13125.e: The dead were supposed to have everything they needed in the afterlife. So they were given many everyday things.
13125.m: The dead were given food, furniture and jewellery in their tombs.

13126.q: What is the collection of magic spells written on papyrus and given to the dead called?
13126.e: The Book of the Dead was meant to help the dead survive the dangers of the afterlife. It contained spells and pictures.
13126.m: The Book of the Dead helped the dead on their way into the afterlife.

13127.e: Hieroglyphs are signs that look like small pictures. The ancient Egyptians wrote with them.
13127.m: Hieroglyphs are the picture writing of the ancient Egyptians.

13128.e: The word comes from Greek. The Greeks saw the signs mainly on temples.

13129.q: Roughly how many different hieroglyph signs were there?
13129.e: For a long time the Egyptians used about 700 different signs. That is far more than the 26 letters of our alphabet.
13129.m: There were several hundred different hieroglyph signs.

13130.q: Who could read and write hieroglyphs in ancient Egypt?
13130.e: Only a few people could read and write. Scribes studied for many years and were highly respected.
13130.m: Scribes were important and respected people in ancient Egypt.

13131.q: What did Egyptian scribes use to write on papyrus?
13131.e: The writing brush was made from a plant stem. Black ink was made from soot.
13131.m: The scribes wrote with a brush and ink.

13132.q: Where can you still find many hieroglyphs today?
13132.e: The Egyptians carved and painted hieroglyphs on the walls of temples and tombs. Many are still well preserved today.
13132.m: Many hieroglyphs are on temples and in tombs.

13133.q: In which direction could hieroglyphs be written?
13133.e: Hieroglyphs could run from right to left, from left to right or from top to bottom. Human and animal figures face the beginning of the text.
13133.m: Hieroglyphs could be written in several directions.

13134.q: What is the oval frame in which a pharaoh's name is written called?
13134.e: The cartouche is a ring around the royal name. It was meant to protect the pharaoh's name.
13134.m: A pharaoh's name is written in a cartouche.

13135.q: Which famous stone helped people to read hieroglyphs again?
13135.e: The Rosetta Stone has the same text in several scripts. Because people could read Greek, they could compare it with the hieroglyphs.
13135.m: The Rosetta Stone helped to decipher hieroglyphs.

13136.q: In how many different scripts is the text on the Rosetta Stone written?
13136.e: The text is written in hieroglyphs, in an everyday Egyptian script and in Greek. That was the key to the solution.
13136.m: The Rosetta Stone has the same text in three scripts.

13137.q: Who was the first to decipher hieroglyphs?
13137.e: Champollion was a French scholar. About 200 years ago he worked out how hieroglyphs work. Other researchers had paved the way for him.
13137.m: Champollion was the first to decipher hieroglyphs.

13138.q: In which city is the Rosetta Stone on display today?
13138.e: The Rosetta Stone is in the British Museum in London. It is one of the best-known objects there.
13138.m: The Rosetta Stone is in London today.

13139.q: How many gods did the ancient Egyptians believe in?
13139.e: The Egyptians worshipped a great many gods. Each god was responsible for something particular, for example the sun or the Nile.
13139.m: The ancient Egyptians believed in a great many gods.

13140.q: What was the Egyptian sun god called?
13140.e: The Egyptians believed that Ra travelled across the sky in a boat every day. He was often shown with a falcon's head and a sun disc.
13140.m: The Egyptian sun god was called Ra.

13141.q: Which god ruled the realm of the dead and is often shown with green skin?
13141.e: Osiris was the god of the dead and of rebirth. The green colour stands for new life, as with plants.
13141.m: Osiris was the ruler of the realm of the dead.

13142.q: What was the name of the wife of the god Osiris, a powerful goddess of magic?
13142.e: Isis was seen as a loving mother and a great magician. According to legend, she brought Osiris back to life.
13142.m: Isis was the wife of Osiris and a powerful goddess.

13143.q: Which of these gods is shown with the head of a falcon?
13143.e: Horus was a sky god and was often shown as a falcon. The pharaoh was regarded as his representative on earth.
13143.m: Horus is the god with the falcon's head.

13144.q: Which goddess was shown as a cat or with a cat's head?
13144.e: Bastet was a protective goddess of the home and family. Many cats were kept in her honour.
13144.m: Bastet is the goddess with the cat's head.

13145.q: Which god with the head of an ibis bird was the god of scribes?
13145.e: Thoth was the god of wisdom and writing. Scribes asked him for help with their work.
13145.m: Thoth with the ibis head was the god of writing.

13146.q: Which of these goddesses is often shown with cow's horns and a sun disc?
13146.e: Hathor was the goddess of love, music and dance. She was also shown as a cow.
13146.m: Hathor is the goddess with the cow's horns.

13147.q: Which god stood for the desert, storms and disorder?
13147.e: In the legends Seth was the evil brother of Osiris. He fought Horus for power.
13147.m: Seth was the god of the desert and disorder.

13148.q: Which goddess with a lion's head was thought to be wild and dangerous?
13148.e: Sekhmet was a goddess of war with a lion's head. But she could also heal diseases.
13148.m: Sekhmet is the wild goddess with the lion's head.

13149.q: Which beetle was sacred to the Egyptians and a symbol of the sun?
13149.e: The scarab rolls balls along in front of it. This made the Egyptians think of the sun rolling across the sky.
13149.m: The scarab was a sacred beetle and a symbol of the sun.

13150.q: According to Egyptian belief, what was a dead person's heart weighed against?
13150.e: The heart was weighed against the feather of the goddess Maat. If it was light, the dead person could enter the afterlife.
13150.m: In the afterlife the heart was weighed against a feather.

13151.q: What does the Egyptian sign ankh, which looks like a cross with a loop, mean?
13151.e: The ankh was a symbol of life. Gods hold it in their hands in many pictures.
13151.m: The ankh sign stands for life.

13152.q: Roughly how old was Tutankhamun when he became pharaoh?
13152.e: Tutankhamun was only about 8 or 9 years old when he became king. That is why experienced advisers helped him to rule.
13152.m: Tutankhamun became pharaoh as a child.

13153.q: Roughly how old was Tutankhamun when he died?
13153.e: Tutankhamun died as a young man of about 18 to 20. Exactly what he died of is still not completely certain.

13154.q: Who discovered the tomb of Tutankhamun?
13154.e: Howard Carter was an English archaeologist. He searched for the tomb for many years.
13154.m: Howard Carter discovered the tomb of Tutankhamun.

13155.q: When was the tomb of Tutankhamun discovered?
13155.e: The tomb was found in 1922. The discovery became known all over the world.
13155.m: The tomb of Tutankhamun was discovered about 100 years ago.

13156.q: Where is the tomb of Tutankhamun?
a: In the Valley of the Kings
In the Great Pyramid of Khufu
On an island in the sea
13156.e: The tomb is in the Valley of the Kings near Luxor. It was hidden under rubble.
13156.m: Tutankhamun's tomb is in the Valley of the Kings.

13157.q: Why is the tomb of Tutankhamun so famous?
a: It was almost untouched and full of treasure
It is the largest tomb in the world
It is built of pure silver
13157.e: Most pharaohs' tombs had been completely robbed long ago. In Tutankhamun's tomb, however, there were still over 5000 objects.
13157.m: Tutankhamun's tomb was almost untouched and full of treasure.

13158.q: What is Tutankhamun's famous death mask made of?
13158.e: The mask is made of gold and decorated with colourful stones and glass. It lay directly on the face of the mummy.
13158.m: Tutankhamun's death mask is made of gold.

13159.q: How many human-shaped coffins lay one inside the other in Tutankhamun's tomb?
13159.e: The three coffins fitted inside each other like nesting dolls and lay in a large stone coffin. The innermost coffin is made of gold.
13159.m: Tutankhamun lay in three coffins; the innermost is gold.

13160.q: Which wealthy Englishman paid for the search for Tutankhamun's tomb?
13160.e: Lord Carnarvon paid for excavations in Egypt for many years. He was there when the tomb was opened.
13160.m: Lord Carnarvon paid for the search for Tutankhamun's tomb.

13161.q: Which vehicles were found in Tutankhamun's tomb?
13161.e: The tomb held several light two-wheeled vehicles. They were pulled by horses and are called chariots.
13161.m: Chariots were found in Tutankhamun's tomb.

13162.q: In which country can you see Tutankhamun's treasures today?
13162.e: The famous death mask and most of the treasures are in the Grand Egyptian Museum near Cairo. Only rarely do individual pieces travel abroad for exhibitions.
13162.m: Tutankhamun's treasures are in Egypt today.

13163.q: What is the ‘curse of the pharaoh’?
13163.e: After the discovery, newspapers claimed that a curse would strike the researchers. It is a legend, because the man who discovered the tomb lived for many more years.
13163.m: The curse of the pharaoh is just a legend.

13164.e: Greece lies in the south of Europe on the Mediterranean. Summers there are hot and dry.

13165.q: Roughly how many islands does Greece have?
a: A great many, over a thousand
13165.e: Greece has a great many islands, for example Crete. That is why the ancient Greeks were good sailors.
13165.m: Greece has a great many islands.

13166.q: What was a Greek city state called?
13166.e: The ancient Greeks lived in many small city states. A city state like this was called a polis. The agora, on the other hand, was the marketplace.
13166.m: A Greek city state was called a polis.

13167.q: Which poet told of Odysseus and his wanderings?
13167.e: The Odyssey is attributed to the poet Homer. It tells of Odysseus's long journey home.
13167.m: Homer told of the wanderings of Odysseus.

13168.q: According to legend, how did the Greeks get into the city of Troy?
13168.e: According to legend, warriors hid inside a large wooden horse. The Trojans pulled it into the city themselves.
13168.m: In the legend, a wooden horse helped the Greeks capture Troy.

13169.q: What are the first two letters of the Greek alphabet?
13169.e: The Greek alphabet begins with alpha and beta. That is where our word ‘alphabet’ comes from. Omega is the last letter.
13169.m: The word alphabet comes from alpha and beta.

13170.q: What did the ancient Greeks invent to show stories on a stage?
13170.e: The Greeks built large open-air theatres. The seats were arranged in a semicircle on a hillside.
13170.m: The theatre comes from ancient Greece.

13171.q: What did actors in Greek theatre wear over their faces?
13171.e: The actors wore masks. That way you could see from far away whether a character was happy or sad.

13172.q: Which trees did the ancient Greeks plant especially often?
13172.e: Olive trees grow well in warm Greece. The olives were used to make oil for cooking and for lamps.
13172.m: The Greeks planted many olive trees.

13173.q: What did the ancient Greeks keep oil and wine in?
13173.e: The Greeks used jars made of clay, for example the amphora. Many of them are beautifully painted.
13173.m: Oil and wine went into clay jars.

13174.q: What stands all around the building in Greek temples?
13174.e: Greek temples have many stone columns. This style of building was often copied later.

13175.q: Where did the Greeks go to ask the gods about the future?
13175.e: There was a famous oracle at Delphi. There a priestess, the Pythia, spoke in the name of the god Apollo.
13175.m: At the Oracle of Delphi people asked about the future.

13176.q: According to a story, which Greek shouted ‘Eureka’ in the bath?
13176.e: Archimedes was a clever scientist. ‘Eureka’ means ‘I have found it’.
13176.m: Archimedes shouted ‘Eureka’, which means ‘I have found it’.

13177.q: What was the name of a well-known Greek thinker from Athens who asked people lots of questions?
13177.e: Socrates lived in Athens and asked people lots of questions. He wanted them to think for themselves.
13177.m: Socrates was a Greek thinker from Athens.

13178.q: What is the famous race that recalls a legend from Greece called?
13178.e: According to legend, a messenger ran from Marathon to Athens to report a victory. The long race is named after the place Marathon.
13178.m: The marathon is named after the place Marathon.

13179.e: The Romans gradually conquered Greece. They admired Greek art and took over a lot of it.
13179.m: Greece was later conquered by the Romans.

13180.q: Which Greek doctor is regarded as the father of medicine?
13180.e: Hippocrates was a famous doctor in ancient Greece. He is regarded as the father of medicine.
13180.m: Hippocrates is regarded as the father of medicine.

13181.q: What is the capital of Greece?
13181.e: Athens is the capital of Greece today. Even in ancient times Athens was a very important city.
13181.m: Athens is the capital of Greece.

13182.q: Which goddess is Athens named after?
13182.e: According to legend, the city was named after the goddess Athena. Athena was the protector of Athens.
13182.m: Athens is named after the goddess Athena.

13183.q: What is the fortified hill in the middle of Athens called?
13183.e: The Acropolis is a rock in the middle of Athens. Famous temples stand on top of it.
13183.m: The Acropolis is the fortified hill of Athens.

13184.q: What is the great temple on the Acropolis called?
13184.e: The Parthenon is a great temple for the goddess Athena. It stands on the Acropolis.
13184.m: The Parthenon stands on the Acropolis.

13185.q: Which form of rule by the people developed in ancient Athens?
13185.e: In Athens citizens could have their say in the people's assembly. The word democracy means ‘rule by the people’.

13186.q: Who was allowed to vote in the people's assembly in ancient Athens?
a: Only adult men who were citizens
13186.e: Only adult male citizens could vote. Women, slaves and foreigners had no say.
13186.m: In Athens only male citizens voted.

13187.q: Which bird was the symbol of Athens?
13187.e: The owl belonged to the goddess Athena. It also appeared on the coins of Athens.
13187.m: The owl was the symbol of Athens.

13188.q: According to legend, what gift did Athena give the city of Athens?
13188.e: According to legend, Athena and Poseidon competed for the city. Athena gave an olive tree and won.
13188.m: According to legend, Athena gave the city an olive tree.

13189.q: What was the marketplace in ancient Athens called?
13189.e: The agora was the marketplace of Athens. People went shopping there and met to talk.
13189.m: The marketplace of Athens was called the agora.

13190.q: What is the port of Athens called?
13190.e: Piraeus is the port of Athens. The Athenians' ships set sail from there.
13190.m: Piraeus is the port of Athens.

13191.q: Which famous politician had the Parthenon built?
13191.e: Pericles was an important politician in Athens. Under him the temples on the Acropolis were built.

13192.q: What did the Athenians vote with when they wanted to banish someone from the city?
13192.e: The Athenians scratched a name onto a piece of broken pottery. Whoever got the most votes had to leave the city for ten years.
13192.m: In Athens people voted on banishment with pieces of pottery.

13193.q: Who usually learned to read and write in ancient Athens?
13193.e: It was mainly boys from rich families who went to school. Girls usually learned housekeeping at home.
13193.m: In Athens it was mainly rich boys who went to school.

13194.q: Which Greek city was for a long time the great rival of Athens?
13194.e: Athens and Sparta were the two most powerful cities in Greece. They fought a long war against each other.
13194.m: Sparta was the great rival of Athens.

13195.q: Where in Switzerland do citizens still vote in the open air today, a bit like in ancient Athens?
13195.e: Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden still have the Landsgemeinde, an open-air assembly. There people vote in the open air by raising their hands.
13195.m: At the Landsgemeinde, Swiss citizens vote directly.

13196.q: What could you see in Athens at the foot of the Acropolis?
13196.e: On the slope of the Acropolis lies the Theatre of Dionysus. Plays were performed there.
13196.m: There was a theatre at the foot of the Acropolis.

13197.q: Which thinker founded a famous school called the Academy in Athens?
13197.e: Plato was a pupil of Socrates. He founded a school in Athens called the Academy.
13197.m: Plato founded the Academy in Athens.

13198.q: What was Sparta especially known for?
13198.e: The Spartans were famous warriors. Their whole life revolved around fighting.
13198.m: Sparta was known for its warriors.

13199.e: Sparta lay in the south of Greece on the Peloponnese peninsula.

13200.q: At what age did Spartan boys begin their tough training?
13200.e: At about seven, the boys had to leave their families. They were brought up in groups to be warriors.
13200.m: Spartan boys began their training at about seven.

13201.q: How many kings did Sparta have at the same time?
13201.e: Sparta always had two kings at the same time. They also led the army in war.
13201.m: Sparta had two kings at the same time.

13202.q: Which king of Sparta fought at Thermopylae?
13202.e: King Leonidas and his warriors defended a narrow pass called Thermopylae. He died there in battle.

13203.q: According to the well-known story, how many Spartans fought with Leonidas?
13203.e: 300 Spartans fought with Leonidas. They were joined by warriors from other Greek cities.

13204.q: Which people did the Spartans fight at Thermopylae?
13204.e: The great Persian army wanted to conquer Greece. The Spartans stood in its way.
13204.m: At Thermopylae the Spartans fought the Persians.

13205.q: What does the word ‘spartan’ mean today?
13205.e: The Spartans lived very simply. That is why today we call something ‘spartan’ when it is very plain.
13205.m: Today spartan means simple and frugal.

13206.q: What shape was a Spartan warrior's shield?
13206.e: The warriors carried a large round shield. With it they protected themselves and their neighbour in the line.
13206.m: Spartan warriors carried a round shield.

13207.q: What did girls in Sparta do differently from girls in Athens?
a: They did a lot of sport
They always had to stay indoors
They only learned weaving and spinning
They were never allowed out on the street
13207.e: In Sparta girls also did sport, such as running and wrestling. In Athens girls mostly stayed at home.
13207.m: In Sparta girls also did a lot of sport.

13208.q: What were the people who had to work the fields in Sparta called?
13208.e: The helots were people who were not free. They had to work in the fields for the Spartans.
13208.m: In Sparta the unfree helots worked the fields.

13209.q: What kind of soup are the Spartans said to have eaten?
13209.e: The Spartans are said to have eaten a black soup. It was simple and foreigners did not like the taste.
13209.m: The Spartans are said to have eaten a black soup.

13210.q: How did the Spartans like to talk?
13210.e: The Spartans spoke briefly and to the point. Their region was called Laconia, which is why today we call short answers ‘laconic’.
13210.m: The Spartans spoke with few words.

13211.q: What colour were the cloaks of Spartan warriors?
13211.e: The Spartans wore red cloaks. You could recognise them from far away.

13212.q: How did Spartan warriors stand in battle?
13212.e: The warriors stood close together in rows. This way their shields formed a wall.
13212.m: Spartan warriors fought in a tight line.

13213.q: What is there today on the site of ancient Sparta?
13213.e: Today there is the town of Sparti there. Only a few ruins remain of ancient Sparta.
13213.m: Only a few ruins remain of ancient Sparta.

13214.q: Who was the king of the Greek gods?
13214.e: Zeus was the highest god. He ruled over the sky and the other gods.
13214.m: Zeus was the king of the gods.

13215.q: On which mountain did the Greek gods live?
13215.e: According to the legends, the gods lived on Mount Olympus. It is the highest mountain in Greece.
13215.m: The Greek gods lived on Mount Olympus.

13216.q: What did Zeus throw when he was angry?
13216.e: Zeus was the god of the sky and the weather. When he was angry, he hurled thunderbolts.

13217.q: Who was the god of the sea?
13217.e: Poseidon ruled the sea. He could cause storms and earthquakes.
13217.m: Poseidon was the god of the sea.

13218.q: What did Poseidon carry in his hand?
13218.e: Poseidon carries a trident, a fork with three prongs. With it he could stir up the sea.

13219.e: Hades was the god of the underworld. According to the Greeks, that is where the dead went.

13220.q: Who was the wife of Zeus?
13220.e: Hera was the wife of Zeus and queen of the gods. She protected marriage.
13220.m: Hera was the wife of Zeus.

13221.q: According to legend, from which part of Zeus's body was Athena born?
13221.e: According to legend, Athena sprang fully armed from the head of Zeus. She was the goddess of wisdom.
13221.m: According to legend, Athena came from the head of Zeus.

13222.q: Who was the goddess of love and beauty?
13222.e: Aphrodite was the goddess of love and beauty. The Romans called her Venus.
13222.m: Aphrodite was the goddess of love.

13223.q: Who was the messenger of the gods with wings on his shoes?
13223.e: Hermes delivered the gods' messages. Thanks to his winged shoes he was very fast.
13223.m: Hermes was the swift messenger of the gods.

13224.q: Who was the god of war?
13224.e: Ares was the wild god of war. The Romans called him Mars.
13224.m: Ares was the god of war.

13225.q: Who was the goddess of hunting?
13225.e: Artemis hunted in the forests with a bow and arrow. She was the twin sister of Apollo.
13225.m: Artemis was the goddess of hunting.

13226.q: Who was the god of music, who often played a lyre?
13226.e: Apollo was the god of music and light. He played the lyre, a stringed instrument.
13226.m: Apollo was the god of music.

13227.q: Which god was a blacksmith and worked with fire?
13227.e: Hephaestus was the god of fire and of smiths. He made weapons and jewellery for the gods.
13227.m: Hephaestus was the blacksmith of the gods.

13228.q: Who was the goddess of the harvest and grain?
13228.e: Demeter made sure that grain grew. Farmers prayed to her for a good harvest.
13228.m: Demeter was the goddess of the harvest.

13229.q: Which hero was the son of Zeus and very strong?
13229.e: Heracles, also called Hercules, was a son of Zeus. According to legend, he had to complete twelve difficult labours.
13229.m: Heracles was a very strong son of Zeus.

13230.q: According to the Greeks, how many main gods lived on Mount Olympus?
13230.e: People speak of the twelve Olympian gods. They include, for example, Zeus, Hera and Athena.
13230.m: Twelve main gods lived on Mount Olympus.

13231.q: Where were the Olympic Games of the ancient Greeks held?
13231.e: The Games of the ancient Greeks took place in Olympia. The Olympic Games are named after this place.
13231.m: The Olympic Games are named after the place Olympia.

13232.q: In honour of which god were the Games in Olympia held?
13232.e: The Games in Olympia were a festival for Zeus. A great temple of Zeus stood in Olympia.
13232.m: The Games in Olympia were held in honour of Zeus.

13233.q: How often were the Games in Olympia held?
13233.e: The Games took place every four years. It is still like that with the Olympic Games today.
13233.m: The Olympic Games take place every four years.

13234.q: What did a winner in Olympia receive as a prize?
13234.e: The winner received a wreath made from the branches of an olive tree. He was then celebrated in his home town.
13234.m: In Olympia the prize was an olive wreath.

13235.q: Which was the only contest in Olympia at the beginning?
13235.e: For a long time there was only one short race through the stadium in Olympia. Other sports were added later.
13235.m: The first contest in Olympia was a footrace.

13236.q: Who was allowed to take part as an athlete in the Games in Olympia?
13236.e: Only free Greek men and boys could compete as athletes. There were separate races for women in honour of the goddess Hera.
13236.m: In Olympia only men and boys could compete as athletes.

13237.q: What was supposed to exist between the Greek cities during the Games in Olympia?
13237.e: A truce was declared. That way athletes and spectators could travel safely to Olympia.
13237.m: During the Games there was supposed to be peace.

13238.q: Which contest with horses was popular in Olympia?
13238.e: In the chariot race, horses pulled a small cart. The races were fast and dangerous.
13238.m: There were chariot races with horses in Olympia.

13239.q: Which combat sport was there in Olympia?
13239.e: In wrestling, two athletes tried to throw each other to the ground. It was already very popular in Olympia.
13239.m: Wrestling was a sport in Olympia.

13240.q: Which throwing objects did the athletes in Olympia use?
13240.e: The athletes threw the discus, a round disc, and the javelin. Both sports still exist today.
13240.m: In Olympia athletes threw the discus and the javelin.

13241.q: Where is the Olympic flame lit today?
13241.e: The flame is lit in Olympia using the sun. Then it is carried with a torch to the new Games.
13241.m: The Olympic flame is lit in Olympia.

13242.q: In which city were the first modern Olympic Games held?
13242.e: The first modern Olympic Games took place in Athens in 1896. This was a way of remembering the ancient Games in Greece.
13242.m: The first modern Olympic Games took place in Athens.

13243.q: Where did the runners in Olympia race each other?
13243.e: Olympia had a stadium with a long straight running track. Spectators sat on the slopes beside it.
13243.m: The runners in Olympia raced in the stadium.

13376.q: What was the ceremony called in which a young man became a knight?
13376.e: First, a sword was solemnly fastened to the young man’s belt. Later he received a light tap with a sword: the accolade, or knighting.
13376.m: With the accolade, a young man became a knight.

13377.q: What do you call a shirt made of lots of small metal rings?
13377.e: Chain mail is made of thousands of small iron rings. It protected the knight from blows.
13377.m: Chain mail is made of small metal rings.

13378.q: What was the fighting contest called in which knights showed their skills?
13378.e: At a tournament, knights competed against each other. Spectators came to watch.
13378.m: At a tournament, knights showed how well they could fight.

13379.q: Which long weapon did a knight carry on horseback?
13379.e: The lance is a long pole with a point. With it the knight charged forward on his horse.
13379.m: A knight fought on horseback with a lance.

13380.q: What did the picture on a knight’s shield show?
13380.e: In battle you often couldn’t see the knight’s face. You could tell who he was by his coat of arms.
13380.m: You recognised a knight by his coat of arms.

13381.e: Many knights lived in castles. From there they protected their land.
13381.m: Many knights lived in a castle.

13382.e: The knight wore a metal helmet. It protected his head in battle.
13382.m: The helmet protected the knight’s head.

13383.q: What do you call the metal clothing that protected a knight?
13383.e: Armour was made of metal and protected the body. It was heavy.
13383.m: Armour protected the knight in battle.

13384.q: What is the ditch around many castles called?
13384.e: A moat made it hard for enemies to reach the walls. Some moats were filled with water.
13384.m: The moat protected the castle from enemies.

13385.q: Which bridge at a castle could be pulled up?
13385.e: The drawbridge led across the moat. When there was danger, it was pulled up.
13385.m: The drawbridge could be pulled up when there was danger.

13386.q: What is the tallest tower of a castle called?
13386.e: The keep was the tall main tower. From the top you could see far across the land.
13386.m: The keep is the tallest tower of a castle.

13387.q: Why were many castles built on hills or rocks?
a: Because there was more water there
To be closer to the market
13387.e: On a hill it was hard for enemies to attack. You could also see them coming from far away.
13387.m: Castles on hills were well protected.

13388.q: What were most castles built from?
13388.e: Castles were mostly built from stone. Thick stone walls were strong.
13388.m: Most castles are built of stone.

13389.q: On which lake does the famous Chillon Castle stand?
13389.e: Chillon Castle stands near Montreux on Lake Geneva. It is a castle on a rock in the water.
13389.m: Chillon Castle is on Lake Geneva.

13390.q: In which canton is Habsburg Castle?
13390.e: Habsburg Castle stands in the canton of Aargau. The famous Habsburg family came from here.

13391.q: Why was the well in a castle especially important?
a: It was used as a hiding place
13391.e: During a siege, nobody could leave the castle. That is why it needed its own well for water.
13391.m: A well gave the castle its own water.

13392.e: Many castles were abandoned and fell apart. What is left is called a ruin.
13392.m: A ruin is a building that has fallen apart.

13393.q: What do you call the lord who owns a castle?
13393.e: The lord of the castle owned it. He lived there with his family.
13393.m: The lord of the castle is its owner.

13394.q: What are the notches along the top of a castle wall called?
13394.e: At the top of the wall, raised parts and gaps take turns. Defenders could shelter behind the battlements.
13394.m: Battlements are the notches along the top of a castle wall.

13395.q: Which people were the most common in the Middle Ages?
13395.e: By far most people were peasants. They grew the food for everyone.
13395.m: In the Middle Ages, most people were peasants.

13396.q: Which animal often pulled the plough in the Middle Ages?
13396.e: Oxen are strong and patient. They pulled the plough across the field.

13397.q: What did peasants have to give their lord?
13397.e: Peasants had to pay dues. They often gave part of their harvest or some animals.
13397.m: Peasants had to give their lord part of the harvest.

13398.q: What was the payment of one tenth of the harvest called?
13398.e: The tithe was one tenth of the harvest. It usually went to the Church.
13398.m: The tithe was the tenth part of the harvest.

13399.q: What was the unpaid work that peasants had to do for their lord called?
13399.e: In labour service, peasants worked on the lord’s fields without pay. The tithe, on the other hand, was a payment from the harvest.
13399.m: Labour service was unpaid work for the lord.

13400.q: Which grain did peasants often grow in the Middle Ages?
13400.e: Rye, wheat, barley and oats were important. Maize only came to Europe later, from America.
13400.m: Grain such as rye was very important in the Middle Ages.

13401.q: What did peasants eat every day in the Middle Ages?
13401.e: Peasants mainly ate grain porridge and bread. Meat was rare, and potatoes were not yet known.
13401.m: In the Middle Ages, peasants ate a lot of porridge and bread.

13402.q: Where did animals and peasants often sleep in winter?
13402.e: People and animals often lived in the same house. The animals kept the house warm.
13402.m: Peasants and animals often lived under one roof.

13403.q: What did people use to cut the grain at harvest time?
13403.e: The sickle is a curved knife. With it people cut the stalks.
13403.m: Grain was cut with a sickle.

13404.q: What did peasant children usually do in the Middle Ages?
a: They went to school every day
They learned to read in a monastery
13404.e: Peasant children had to help from an early age. They looked after animals or helped in the fields. Very few went to school.
13404.m: In the Middle Ages, peasant children helped with the work from an early age.

13405.q: What were the roofs of many farmhouses made of?
13405.e: Many simple houses had roofs made of straw or reeds. The material was cheap. Tiles and stone slabs were more expensive.
13405.m: Many farmhouses had a thatched straw roof.

13406.q: What surrounded a medieval town to protect it?
13406.e: The town wall protected the people from enemies. You could only get in through the gates.
13406.m: A town wall protected the medieval town.

13407.q: What happened to the town gates at night?
13407.e: In the evening the gates were closed. That way nobody could get into the town at night.
13407.m: The town gates were closed at night.

13408.q: Where did people in a town do their shopping?
13408.e: In the market square, farmers and traders sold their goods. The market was very important for a town.
13408.m: In the Middle Ages, people shopped at the market.

13409.q: Which Swiss town was founded by the Dukes of Zähringen?
13409.e: Bern was founded by the Zähringen family. Fribourg is also a Zähringen town.
13409.m: Bern was founded by the Zähringen family.

13410.q: What were the free inhabitants of a town called?
13410.e: The citizens lived in the town and had certain rights. The German word for them, “Bürger”, comes from “Burg” (castle).
13410.m: The free inhabitants of a town were called citizens.

13411.q: Where did some people in the Middle Ages throw their rubbish?
13411.e: There was no rubbish collection like today. A lot of dirt simply ended up in the streets.
13411.m: The streets in the Middle Ages were often dirty.

13412.q: Who guarded the town at night and called out the hours?
13412.e: The night watchman walked through the streets. He watched out for fires and thieves.
13412.m: The night watchman looked after the town at night.

13413.q: Why were fires so dangerous in medieval towns?
a: Many houses were made of wood
The walls were made of stone
13413.e: Many houses were made of wood and stood close together. A fire could spread quickly.
13413.m: Wooden houses burned easily in the Middle Ages.

13414.q: Which building in the middle of the town was often the biggest?
13414.e: Large churches and minsters towered over the houses. You could see them from far away.
13414.m: The church was often the biggest building in town.

13415.q: Where did the men who governed a town meet?
13415.e: The town council met in the town hall. It made rules for the citizens.
13415.m: The town was governed from the town hall.

13416.q: What were the streets in medieval towns usually like?
13416.e: There was little space behind the wall. That is why the streets were narrow and crooked.

13417.q: Who made horseshoes and iron tools in the Middle Ages?
13417.e: The blacksmith heated iron in the fire and shaped it with a hammer.
13417.m: The blacksmith shaped iron with a hammer.

13418.e: The shoemaker, also called a cobbler, sewed shoes out of leather.
13418.m: The shoemaker made shoes out of leather.

13419.e: The miller ground the grain into flour in the mill. The mill was often driven by water.
13419.m: The miller ground the grain into flour.

13420.q: Who made pots and jugs out of clay?
13420.e: The potter shaped clay and fired it in a kiln. That made it hard.
13420.m: The potter made pots out of clay.

13421.q: What was a young person learning a craft called?
13421.e: First you were an apprentice with a master. There you learned the craft.

13422.q: What was a craftsman called after finishing his apprenticeship?
13422.e: After the apprenticeship you became a journeyman. Many journeymen went travelling to work in other places.
13422.m: After the apprenticeship you were a journeyman.

13423.q: What was a craftsman called who was allowed to run his own workshop?
13423.e: A master had his own workshop. He trained apprentices.
13423.m: A master ran his own workshop.

13424.q: What are the associations of craftsmen in a town called?
13424.e: In a guild, craftsmen of the same trade came together. They made rules for their craft.

13425.q: In which Swiss city is the Böögg burned at the Sechseläuten festival?
13425.e: Sechseläuten is a spring festival in Zurich. The craftsmen’s guilds parade through the city in old costumes, and at the end the Böögg burns.

13426.q: Who built houses out of stone?
13426.e: The mason laid stones on top of each other. He built walls, churches and castles.

13427.e: The tailor cut cloth and sewed clothes from it.

13428.q: What are men who live in a monastery called?
13428.e: Monks live in a monastery and dedicate their lives to God. They pray and work.

13429.q: What are women who live in a convent called?
13429.e: Nuns live in a convent. They also pray and work.

13430.q: What is the head of a monastery called?
13430.e: The abbot leads the monastery. The monks obey him.
13430.m: The abbot is the head of a monastery.

13431.q: What did monks often do with books?
a: They sold them at the market
13431.e: Books were copied by hand. That often took a long time.

13432.q: What does the well-known Benedictine motto “ora et labora” mean?
13432.e: “Ora et labora” is Latin. The phrase only appeared later, but it sums up well how monks were meant to live: praying and working.
13432.m: The Benedictines live by the motto “Pray and work”.

13433.q: Which Swiss town has a famous monastery with an old library?
13433.e: The Abbey Library of St Gallen owns very old books. It is a World Heritage Site.
13433.m: There is a famous abbey library in St Gallen.

13434.q: In which place in the canton of Schwyz is there a large, famous monastery?
13434.e: Einsiedeln Abbey is in the canton of Schwyz. Many people travel there to pray.
13434.m: There is a famous monastery in Einsiedeln.

13435.q: What did monks grow in the monastery garden?
13435.e: Herbs, vegetables and fruit grew in the monastery garden. Some herbs were used as medicine.
13435.m: Herbs and vegetables grew in the monastery garden.

13436.q: Where did the monks pray together?
13436.e: Several times a day the monks went to the church to pray.
13436.m: Monks prayed in church several times a day.

13437.q: Who often looked after sick people in the Middle Ages?
13437.e: Many monasteries cared for the sick and the poor. They knew about healing herbs.
13437.m: In the Middle Ages, monasteries helped the sick and the poor.

13438.q: In which language did monks usually pray and write?
13438.e: The language of the Church was Latin. Many books in the monastery were in Latin.
13438.m: In the monastery, people often spoke and wrote Latin.

13439.q: Which region did the Vikings come from?
13439.e: The Vikings came from the north of Europe. Today Denmark, Norway and Sweden are there.

13442.q: Did Viking helmets have horns in battle?
13442.e: Viking helmets that have been found have no horns. The horns only appeared about 150 years ago through pictures and operas.
13442.m: Real Viking helmets had no horns.

13443.q: What are the Viking letters called?
13443.e: The Vikings carved runes into stone, wood or bone. Many rune stones still exist today.

13444.q: Which Viking god had a mighty hammer?
13444.e: Thor was the Vikings’ god of thunder. His hammer is called Mjölnir.
13444.m: Thor is the god of thunder with the hammer.

13445.q: Who was the chief god of the Vikings?
13445.e: Odin was the most important god in the Norse myths. He had only one eye.
13445.m: Odin was the chief god of the Vikings.

13447.q: On which large island in the north did the Vikings settle?
13447.e: People from Scandinavia settled in Iceland and later also in Greenland.

13448.q: Apart from fighting, what else did Vikings often do?
13448.e: The Vikings were also traders and farmers. They traded furs, silver and jewellery.
13448.m: The Vikings were also traders and farmers.

13449.q: What did the Vikings often raid because gold and silver were kept there?
13449.e: Monasteries often had gold, silver and valuable books. In the year 793, Vikings raided the monastery of Lindisfarne in England.
13449.m: The Vikings often raided rich monasteries.

13450.e: The plague is a dangerous disease. In the Middle Ages, a great many people died of it.
13450.m: The plague was a dangerous disease.

13451.q: What else is the great plague of the Middle Ages called?
13451.e: The great wave of plague in the Middle Ages is called the Black Death. It struck all of Europe.
13451.m: The great plague is also called the Black Death.

13452.q: Which small creatures often spread the plague?
13452.e: Fleas bit sick animals and then people. That way they could pass on the plague.

13453.q: Which word from the time of the plague means that new arrivals had to wait apart for a while?
13453.e: Because of the plague, travellers and ships had to wait about 40 days in some ports. The word comes from the Italian word for forty.
13453.m: Quarantine means staying apart for a while.

13454.q: About how many people in Europe died of the Black Death?
13454.e: Researchers estimate that around a third of the people in Europe died. Some even think it was more.
13454.m: The Black Death killed about one in three people in Europe.

13455.e: The plague is caused by a bacterium. Bacteria are tiny living things that you can only see with a microscope.

13456.q: How did the plague reach Europe?
13456.e: Traders brought the plague on ships to the ports. From there it spread.
13456.m: The plague came to Europe on trading ships.

13457.q: Did people in the Middle Ages know where the plague came from?
13457.e: People did not know the cause. The bacterium was only discovered much later.
13457.m: In the Middle Ages, people did not know the cause of the plague.

13458.q: What is the form of plague with large swellings called?
13458.e: With bubonic plague, sick people got big swellings on their bodies.

13459.q: Why did the plague spread especially fast in towns?
a: It was always very cold there
13459.e: In towns, many people lived close together. There were also lots of rats and dirt.
13459.m: The plague spread fast in crowded, dirty towns.

13460.q: How did people protect themselves from those who had the plague?
13460.e: Many people fled or stayed away from the sick.
13460.m: Keeping your distance helped protect you from the plague.

13461.q: How many cantons does Switzerland have today?
13461.e: Over time, the first three places grew into a Switzerland with 26 cantons.

13462.e: Confederates were the people of the places that had joined together in an alliance by swearing an oath.
13462.m: Confederates (Eidgenossen) are comrades who are bound by an oath (Eid).

13463.e: If you swear an oath, you promise something very solemnly and seriously. This is where the word Eidgenossenschaft (Confederation) comes from.
13463.m: An oath is a solemn promise.

13464.q: Which town on Lake Lucerne joined the alliance as the fourth place?
13464.e: Lucerne was the first town to join the three forest cantons.
13464.m: Lucerne was the fourth place of the Confederation.

13465.q: Which large town joined the alliance soon after Lucerne?
13465.e: After Lucerne, Zurich joined the alliance. Later came Glarus, Zug and Bern.
13465.m: Zurich joined the Confederation early on.

13466.q: What do people often do on the evening of 1 August?
a: Light a bonfire on a hill
13466.e: On the evening of 1 August, bonfires burn on many hills, and children carry paper lanterns.
13466.m: On 1 August, many bonfires burn in Switzerland.

13467.q: What are the former “places” (Orte) of the Confederation called today?
13467.e: The old places of the Confederation are called cantons today.
13467.m: Today the old places are called cantons.

13468.q: What is the old assembly called where everyone votes outdoors by raising their hand?
13468.e: At the Landsgemeinde, the people who are allowed to vote meet in a square. This old tradition still exists today in Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden.
13468.m: At the Landsgemeinde, people vote in the open air.

13469.q: What did the Old Swiss Confederacy become much later?
13469.e: Over many centuries, the small alliance of the first places grew into today's Switzerland.
13469.m: The Old Swiss Confederacy is the beginning of Switzerland.

13470.q: In which present-day canton is the castle the Habsburgs are named after?
13470.e: Habsburg Castle is in the canton of Aargau. The powerful Habsburg family came from there.
13470.m: The Habsburgs got their name from a castle in Aargau.

13471.q: What is the official name of Switzerland?
13471.e: The official name is still the Swiss Confederation. It is a reminder of the old alliance.
13471.m: Switzerland's official name is the Swiss Confederation.

13472.q: What did the fighters of the places carry with them to show who they were?
13472.e: Each place had its own banner, that is, a flag. This way, people knew who belonged to whom.
13472.m: Each old place had its own flag.

13473.q: What do you call men who fought for foreign rulers in return for pay?
13473.e: Many young Confederates went to foreign countries as mercenaries and fought there for money.
13473.m: Mercenaries fight for pay in a foreign army.

13474.q: Which Swiss troop still protects the Pope in Rome today?
13474.e: The Swiss Guard was founded in the time of the Old Swiss Confederacy and still guards the Pope in the Vatican today.
13474.m: The Swiss Guard protects the Pope.

13475.q: Which three places founded the Swiss Confederation?
13475.e: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden were the first to join together. They are also called the forest cantons.
13475.m: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden are the first three places of Switzerland.

13476.q: What are Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden also called together?
13476.e: Because they stand at the beginning of Switzerland, they are called the original cantons or original Switzerland.
13476.m: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden are called the original cantons.

13477.q: Which animal is on the coat of arms of Uri?
13477.e: The Uri coat of arms shows a black bull's head, the Uri bull.
13477.m: There is a bull's head on the coat of arms of Uri.

13478.q: What background colour does the Uri coat of arms have?
13478.e: The black bull's head of Uri is on a yellow background.
13478.m: The Uri coat of arms is yellow with a black bull's head.

13479.q: Which canton gave Switzerland its name?
13479.e: Other people soon called all the Confederates “Schwyzer”. This is how the name Switzerland came about.
13479.m: The name Switzerland comes from the canton of Schwyz.

13480.q: What does the flag of Schwyz look like?
a: Red with a small white cross
13480.e: The Schwyz flag is red and has a small white cross at the top. It is related to the Swiss flag.
13480.m: The flag of Schwyz is red with a small white cross.

13481.q: Into which two cantons is Unterwalden divided today?
13481.e: Unterwalden is made up of two half-cantons, which today are called cantons: Obwalden and Nidwalden.
13481.m: Unterwalden is made up of Obwalden and Nidwalden.

13482.q: Which object can be seen on the coats of arms of Obwalden and Nidwalden?
13482.e: Obwalden shows a key, Nidwalden a double key.
13482.m: There are keys on the coats of arms of Obwalden and Nidwalden.

13483.q: What is the capital of the canton of Uri called?
13483.e: Altdorf is the capital of Uri. It lies near Lake Uri.
13483.m: Altdorf is the capital of Uri.

13484.q: What is the capital of the canton of Schwyz called?
13484.e: The capital of the canton of Schwyz is also called Schwyz.
13484.m: The canton and its capital are both called Schwyz.

13485.q: What is the capital of Obwalden called?
13485.e: Sarnen is the capital of the canton of Obwalden.
13485.m: Sarnen is the capital of Obwalden.

13486.q: Which famous Alpine pass leads from Uri to Ticino?
13486.e: The Gotthard Pass connects Andermatt in Uri with Airolo in Ticino. An important route through the Alps went over it.
13486.m: The Gotthard Pass leads from Uri to Ticino.

13487.q: Where did the route over the Gotthard lead?
13487.e: Traders crossed the Gotthard from north to south towards Italy. This made Uri important.
13487.m: The Gotthard route connects the north with Italy.

13488.q: On which lake are Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden?
13488.e: All three original cantons border Lake Lucerne. Its German name, Vierwaldstättersee (Lake of the Four Forest Cantons), is a reminder of the forest cantons.
13488.m: The original cantons lie on Lake Lucerne.

13489.q: How did most people in the original cantons make a living back then?
13489.e: Most people were farmers. They kept cows, goats and sheep on pastures and Alpine meadows.
13489.m: The people of original Switzerland were mostly farmers.

13490.q: What does the name “Waldstätte” (forest cantons) mean?
13490.e: The three places lay in valleys with lots of forest. That is why they were called Waldstätte, forest places.
13490.m: The forest cantons were valleys with lots of forest.

13491.q: From which year does the Federal Charter date?
13491.e: The Federal Charter is dated to the year 1291.
13491.m: The Federal Charter dates from the year 1291.

13492.q: In which language is the Federal Charter written?
13492.e: Important documents were often written in Latin back then. The Federal Charter is in Latin too.
13492.m: The Federal Charter is written in Latin.

13493.q: What is the Federal Charter written on?
13493.e: Parchment is a thin, treated animal skin. Important letters were written on it in the Middle Ages.
13493.m: The Federal Charter is written on parchment made from animal skin.

13494.q: Where can you see the real Federal Charter today?
a: In the Museum of the Swiss Charters in Schwyz
In the Federal Palace in Bern
In the National Museum in Zurich
In the town hall in Altdorf
13494.e: The Federal Charter is kept in the Museum of the Swiss Charters of Confederation in Schwyz.
13494.m: The Federal Charter is in the Museum of the Swiss Charters in Schwyz.

13495.e: In the Federal Charter, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden promised each other help. So it is a treaty.
13495.m: The Federal Charter is a treaty of alliance.

13496.q: How long was the alliance meant to last according to the Federal Charter?
13496.e: The Federal Charter says that the alliance should last for ever, God willing.
13496.m: The alliance in the Federal Charter was meant to last for ever.

13497.q: What did the places promise each other in the Federal Charter?
a: To help each other in danger
To pay taxes to the Habsburgs
13497.e: The places promised to help each other against attacks.
13497.m: In the Federal Charter, the places promised to help each other.

13498.q: How was the Federal Charter confirmed?
13498.e: Wax seals hung from the Federal Charter. They were like a signature.
13498.m: In the Middle Ages, seals were like a signature.

13499.q: Which judges did the places not want, according to the Federal Charter?
13499.e: The Federal Charter says that they will not accept a judge who does not come from the valley or who has bought his office.
13499.m: The Confederates did not want foreign judges.

13500.q: About how big is the Federal Charter?
a: About as big as a school exercise book
About as big as a door
About as big as a postage stamp
About as big as a table
13500.e: The Federal Charter is a sheet of about 32 by 20 centimetres. That is about as big as a school exercise book.
13500.m: The Federal Charter is about as big as a school exercise book.

13501.q: What did the Federal Charter do with an older alliance that already existed before?
13501.e: The text says that an older alliance is being renewed. So there was already an agreement before.
13501.m: The Federal Charter renewed an even older alliance.

13502.q: Who was to settle a quarrel between Confederates, according to the Federal Charter?
13502.e: Quarrels were to be settled by the most sensible of the Confederates, not by foreign lords and not by weapons.
13502.m: According to the Federal Charter, wise people were to settle quarrels.

13503.q: What else can you see in the Museum of the Swiss Charters apart from the Federal Charter?
a: The armour of Charles the Bold
13503.e: Old flags and banners from the time of the Confederates also hang in the museum.
13503.m: You can also see old flags in the Museum of the Swiss Charters.

13504.q: With which words does the Federal Charter begin, in translation?
13504.e: The Federal Charter begins in Latin with “In nomine Domini amen”. That means “In the name of God. Amen.”
13504.m: The Federal Charter begins with the words “In the name of God”.

13505.q: From which period does the Federal Charter date?
13505.e: The Federal Charter was written in the Middle Ages, the time of castles and knights.
13505.m: The Federal Charter is a document from the Middle Ages.

13506.q: About how old is the Federal Charter?
13506.e: The Federal Charter was written over 700 years ago. That is a very long time ago.
13506.m: The Federal Charter is over 700 years old.

13507.q: What did William Tell have to shoot off in the legend?
13507.e: In the legend, Tell had to shoot an apple off his son's head.
13507.m: In the Tell legend, Tell shoots an apple off his son's head.

13508.q: Which weapon did Tell shoot with?
13508.e: Tell was a very good shot with the crossbow.
13508.m: William Tell shot with a crossbow.

13509.q: What is the name of the wicked bailiff in the Tell legend?
13509.e: In the legend, the bailiff Gessler was strict and nasty to the people.
13509.m: Gessler is the wicked bailiff in the Tell legend.

13510.q: What did Gessler hang on a pole in the legend?
13510.e: Gessler had his hat put on a pole. Everyone who passed by was supposed to see it.
13510.m: In the legend, Gessler hung his hat on a pole.

13511.q: What were people supposed to do in front of Gessler's hat?
13511.e: Everyone had to bow to the hat. Tell did not, and that is how his story began.
13511.m: Tell refused to bow to Gessler's hat.

13512.q: In which place did the apple shot happen, according to the legend?
13512.e: In the legend, the apple shot takes place in the square in Altdorf in Uri.
13512.m: The apple shot is said to have happened in Altdorf.

13513.q: What is Tell's son called in the best-known Tell story?
13513.e: In the old chronicles, Tell's child has no name yet. Only in the famous play about Tell is the son called Walter, and that is how the story is mostly told today.
13513.m: In the best-known Tell story, Tell's son is called Walter.

a: That has not been proven; he is a legendary figure
Yes, he was the first king of Uri
Yes, his grave is in Altdorf
Yes, he signed the Federal Charter
13514.e: There is no reliable evidence of Tell from his time. He is a figure from a legend.
13514.m: William Tell is a legendary figure; his life has not been proven.

13515.q: What happened to Tell after the apple shot, according to the legend?
13515.e: Gessler had Tell tied up. He was to be taken by boat across the lake to prison.
13515.m: According to the legend, Tell was taken prisoner after the apple shot.

13516.q: In which village in Uri is Tell said to have lived, according to the legend?
13516.e: The legend names Bürglen near Altdorf as Tell's home. There is a Tell Museum there.
13516.m: Tell is said to have come from Bürglen in Uri.

13517.q: Where did Tell defeat the bailiff Gessler, according to the legend?
a: In the Hohle Gasse near Küssnacht
13517.e: According to the legend, Tell lay in wait for Gessler in the Hohle Gasse, a sunken lane near Küssnacht.
13517.m: In the legend, Tell meets Gessler in the Hohle Gasse.

13518.q: How did Tell escape from Gessler's boat in the storm, according to the legend?
a: He jumped onto a flat rock
He swam all the way to Lucerne
13518.e: In the storm, Tell jumped onto a flat rock on the shore. Today it is called the Tellsplatte (Tell's rock).
13518.m: According to the legend, Tell jumped onto the Tellsplatte.

13519.q: Which small church stands where Tell is said to have jumped out of the boat?
13519.e: Tell's Chapel, with pictures from the legend, stands at the Tellsplatte on Lake Uri.
13519.m: Tell's Chapel stands on the shore of Lake Uri.

13520.q: Which writer wrote a famous play about Tell?
13520.e: The German writer Friedrich Schiller wrote the play “William Tell”. It made Tell world-famous.
13520.m: Friedrich Schiller wrote the play “William Tell”.

13521.q: Which composer wrote an opera about William Tell?
13521.e: Rossini wrote the opera “Guillaume Tell”. Lots of people know its fast music at the beginning.
13521.m: Rossini turned the Tell legend into an opera.

13522.q: Where is the famous Tell monument with father and son?
13522.e: The Tell monument in Altdorf shows Tell with his crossbow and his son.
13522.m: The Tell monument is in Altdorf.

13523.q: What was Tell's second arrow meant for, according to the legend?
a: For Gessler, if he hit his child
For a bird in the tree
13523.e: Tell said he would have shot the second arrow at Gessler if he had hit his child.
13523.m: In the legend, the second arrow was meant for Gessler.

13524.q: In which place in the Bernese Oberland is the Tell play performed outdoors every summer?
13524.e: In Interlaken, the Tell plays have been held in the open air for many years.
13524.m: The Tell plays are performed in Interlaken.

13526.e: The Rütli is a meadow above Lake Uri, a part of Lake Lucerne.
13526.m: The Rütli is a meadow by Lake Uri.

13527.q: In which canton is the Rütli?
13527.e: The Rütli belongs to the municipality of Seelisberg in the canton of Uri.
13527.m: The Rütli is in the canton of Uri.

13528.q: How many leaders are said to have sworn the oath on the Rütli, according to legend?
13528.e: The legend tells of three men, one each from Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden.
13528.m: According to legend, three men swore the oath on the Rütli.

13529.q: Which place did Werner Stauffacher come from, according to legend?
13529.e: In the legend, Werner Stauffacher was the representative of Schwyz.
13529.m: According to legend, Werner Stauffacher came from Schwyz.

13530.q: Which place did Walter Fürst come from, according to legend?
13530.e: In the legend, Walter Fürst was the representative of Uri.
13530.m: According to legend, Walter Fürst came from Uri.

13531.q: Which place did Arnold von Melchtal come from, according to legend?
13531.e: In the legend, Arnold von Melchtal represented Unterwalden. The Melchtal valley is in Obwalden.
13531.m: According to legend, Arnold von Melchtal came from Unterwalden.

13532.q: What did the men on the Rütli swear, according to legend?
a: To stand together against the bailiffs
13532.e: They swore to help each other and to defend themselves together against the harsh bailiffs.
13532.m: On the Rütli, the men swore to stand together.

13533.q: At what time of day did the men meet on the Rütli, according to legend?
13533.e: The men met secretly at night.
13533.m: According to legend, the Rütli Oath happened at night.

13534.q: Why did the men meet secretly, according to legend?
a: So that the bailiffs would not notice
Because it was too hot during the day
Because the lake was too rough during the day
Because they wanted to see the stars
13534.e: The bailiffs would have punished them. That is why they met in secret.
13534.m: According to legend, the Rütli Oath was a secret meeting.

13535.q: Has it been proven that the Rütli Oath really happened like this?
a: Yes, there is a letter from that time
Yes, there is a picture from that time
Yes, the men wrote everything down
13535.e: There is no source from that time for the Rütli Oath. The story was only written down much later.
13535.m: The Rütli Oath is a legend and has not been proven.

13536.e: The Rütli was bought a long time ago and given to the Swiss Confederation. So it belongs to everyone.
13536.m: The Rütli belongs to the Swiss Confederation.

13537.q: What takes place on the Rütli on 1 August every year?
13537.e: On the national holiday, there is a celebration on the Rütli with speeches and music.
13537.m: On 1 August, there is a celebration on the Rütli.

13538.q: How do people in Switzerland traditionally hold their hand when swearing an oath?
13538.e: When swearing an oath, you raise your right hand with the thumb, index finger and middle finger. The Rütli Oath is often shown like this too.
13538.m: When swearing an oath, you raise three fingers of your right hand.

13539.q: How does the Rütli Oath begin in the famous play “William Tell”?
a: “We will be a single nation of brothers”
13539.e: In Friedrich Schiller's play “William Tell”, the men on the Rütli swear: “We will be a single nation of brothers”.
13539.m: In the Tell play, the Confederates swear to be a single nation of brothers.

13540.q: Which Swiss general gathered his officers on the Rütli during the Second World War?
13540.e: General Guisan gathered his officers on the Rütli. The place was meant to show courage and unity.
13540.m: General Guisan chose the Rütli as a sign of unity.

13541.q: Who were the bailiffs in the Rütli legend?
13541.e: The bailiffs ran the land for powerful lords. In the legend, they were harsh and unfair.
13541.m: In the Middle Ages, bailiffs ran the land for rulers.

13542.q: Who did the Confederates fight against at Morgarten?
13542.e: At Morgarten, the Confederates fought against an army of the Habsburgs.
13542.m: At Morgarten, the Confederates fought against the Habsburgs.

13543.q: Who won the Battle of Morgarten?
13543.e: The Confederates attacked the Habsburg army on the march and defeated it.
13543.m: The Confederates won the Battle of Morgarten.

13544.e: Morgarten lies on Lake Ägeri, between the lake and the hills.

13545.q: About how many years after the Federal Charter was the Battle of Morgarten?
13545.e: The battle took place in 1315, about 25 years after the Federal Charter.
13545.m: The Battle of Morgarten was about 25 years after the Federal Charter.

13546.q: How did many of the Habsburg fighters go into battle?
13546.e: In the Habsburg army there were many knights in armour who rode on horses.
13546.m: The Habsburgs came with many knights on horseback.

13547.q: What are the Confederates said to have rolled down the slope, according to old reports?
13547.e: Old chronicles say that the Confederates rolled stones and tree trunks down onto the army from above. Today people think they probably mainly threw smaller stones.
13547.m: According to old reports, stones and tree trunks rolled down the slope at Morgarten.

13548.q: What was the name of the Habsburg duke who led the army?
13548.e: Duke Leopold of Habsburg led the army. He survived the defeat.
13548.m: Duke Leopold led the Habsburg army at Morgarten.

13549.q: Why was the place at Morgarten good for the Confederates?
a: The path was narrow between the slope and the lake
There was a big castle there
13549.e: On the narrow path, the knights could hardly move. The Confederates attacked from above.
13549.m: The narrow path at Morgarten helped the Confederates.

13550.q: In which season did the Battle of Morgarten take place?
13550.e: The battle was on 15 November, in late autumn.
13550.m: The Battle of Morgarten was in November.

13551.q: What stands near Morgarten today in memory of the battle?
13551.e: A Morgarten monument stands by Lake Ägeri in memory of the battle.
13551.m: A monument commemorates the Battle of Morgarten.

13552.q: Which monastery did the people of Schwyz quarrel with over pastures and forests before the battle?
13552.e: The people of Schwyz and Einsiedeln Abbey quarrelled over land for a long time. Because the Habsburgs protected the abbey, the quarrel grew.
13552.m: A quarrel with Einsiedeln Abbey was one reason for the Battle of Morgarten.

13553.q: Which long weapon with an axe and a spike did the Confederates often carry?
13553.e: The halberd has a spike, an axe blade and a hook on a long shaft. It was the typical weapon of the Confederates.
13553.m: The halberd was a typical weapon of the Confederates.

13554.q: On the border of which two cantons is Morgarten today?
13554.e: The Morgarten area lies today on the border between the cantons of Zug and Schwyz.
13554.m: Morgarten lies between the cantons of Zug and Schwyz.

13555.q: In which place did the three forest cantons renew their alliance after the battle?
13555.e: A few weeks after the battle, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden made a new alliance in Brunnen.
13555.m: After Morgarten, the forest cantons renewed their alliance in Brunnen.

13556.e: In a battle, two armies fight each other. Often many people are injured or killed.
13556.m: A battle is a fight between two armies.

13557.q: Which event takes place every year in November near Morgarten?
13557.e: At the Morgarten shooting contest, marksmen remember the battle every year in November.
13557.m: At the Morgarten shooting contest, people remember the battle every year.

13558.q: What is the Battle of Morgarten known for?
a: As the first big battle of the Confederates
As the end of the Confederation
As the first battle at sea
As a victory of the Romans
13558.e: Morgarten is seen as the first big battle of the young Confederation. Many stories about it were embellished later.
13558.m: Morgarten is seen as the first big battle of the Confederates.

13559.q: Before printing, how were books in Europe usually made?
13559.e: Before printing, every book had to be copied by hand, letter by letter. That often took months.
13559.m: In the past, books were copied laboriously by hand.

13560.q: Who often copied books by hand in the Middle Ages?
13560.e: Monasteries had writing rooms. There, monks carefully copied books.
13560.m: In monasteries, monks copied many books.

13561.q: Why were books so expensive before printing?
a: Copying them took a very long time
There were only very thin books
They could only be made in winter
Every book had a stone cover
13561.e: A scribe needed many months for a thick book. That is why a book cost a lot of money.
13561.m: Handwritten books were rare and expensive.

13562.e: Pieces of type are small blocks, each with one letter on it. You can put them together again and again to make new words.
13562.m: With movable type you can put together any word.

13563.q: What material was the type made of in printing after Gutenberg?
13563.e: Gutenberg cast his type from a mixture of metals, mainly lead. That made the letters hard and all the same size.
13563.m: Gutenberg’s letters were made of cast metal.

13564.q: Which machine presses the paper onto the type?
13564.e: In the printing press, the paper is pressed firmly onto the inked type. That is how a printed page is made.
13564.m: The printing press presses the paper onto the letters.

13565.q: Which device probably served Gutenberg as the model for his printing press?
13565.e: Gutenberg’s press was probably built on the model of wine presses. A large screw pushed the plate down.
13565.m: The first printing press looked like a wine press.

13566.q: What happened to books once they could be printed?
13566.e: With the printing press, many books could be made in a short time. That is why books became cheaper.
13566.m: Printed books were cheaper than copied ones.

13567.q: Thanks to printing, what became possible for many more people?
13567.e: There were far more printed books than copied ones. So more people could afford a book of their own.
13567.m: Thanks to printing, more people could afford books.

13568.q: What is spread on the type before printing?
13568.e: The type is coated with printing ink. Then the paper is pressed onto it, and the letters appear.
13568.m: Without printing ink there is no print.

13569.q: How does a letter appear on a piece of type?
a: Just like in the finished book
13569.e: When printing, the image is reversed, just like with a stamp. That is why the letter on the type has to be back to front.
13569.m: On a piece of type, the letter is back to front, like on a stamp.

13570.q: Where was printing done long before Gutenberg?
13570.e: In China, books and pictures were printed many hundreds of years earlier. In Korea, too, people printed with movable type before Gutenberg.
13570.m: In China, printing was known long before Gutenberg.

13571.q: What do you call a person who prints books?
13571.e: A printer makes the printed pages. The bookbinder then binds them together into a book.
13571.m: The printer prints the pages of a book.

13572.q: Thanks to printing, what could later be made in large numbers?
13572.e: With printing, news could also be copied quickly. That is how the first newspapers came about later.
13572.m: Thanks to printing, newspapers could later be made.

13573.q: What is the big advantage of a printing press?
a: Decorating every page beautifully by hand
Printing pages with no ink at all
13573.e: Once a page has been set, you can print it the same way many times. That is much faster than copying.
13573.m: A printing press quickly prints many identical pages.

13574.q: In which Swiss city were there many printers early on?
13574.e: The first printing workshop in Switzerland opened in Basel, only around 20 years after Gutenberg’s invention. The city had a university and many scholars.
13574.m: Basel was an important city for printing early on.

13575.e: Paper was cheaper than animal skin and was easy to print on. That is why people usually printed on paper.
13575.m: Printing was usually done on paper.

13576.q: What does a typesetter do in a printing workshop?
a: Puts the type together into words
Sells the books in the shop
13576.e: The typesetter takes the single pieces of type out of a case. He puts them together into words, lines and whole pages.
13576.m: The typesetter puts the letters together into pages.

13577.q: Why is printing considered a very important invention?
13577.e: Printed books and pamphlets reached many people. That way ideas and knowledge could spread quickly.
13577.m: Printing helped knowledge to spread quickly.

13578.q: What did people in Europe often use to print pictures before Gutenberg?
13578.e: A picture was carved into a wooden block, which was inked and printed. This is called a woodcut.
13578.m: Before Gutenberg, pictures were printed with wooden blocks.

13579.e: Around 1450, Gutenberg invented printing with movable type. With it he changed the world.

13580.q: In which city was Gutenberg born?
13580.e: Gutenberg was born in Mainz. Today Mainz is in Germany.

13581.q: Roughly how long did Gutenberg’s workshop work on the Bible?
13581.e: Gutenberg and his helpers worked on the Bible for about two to three years. Every page had to be set letter by letter.
13581.m: Printing the Gutenberg Bible took about two to three years.

a: At the end of the Middle Ages
In the time of the ancient Romans
13582.e: Gutenberg lived around 600 years ago. That was at the end of the Middle Ages.
13582.m: Gutenberg lived at the end of the Middle Ages.

13583.q: Did Gutenberg become rich through his invention?
a: No, he had big money worries
13583.e: Gutenberg had borrowed a lot of money. He lost a court case and had to give up his workshop.
13583.m: Gutenberg did not get rich from his invention.

13584.q: In which language is the Gutenberg Bible printed?
13584.e: At that time the Bible was read in church in Latin. That is why Gutenberg printed it in Latin.
13584.m: The Gutenberg Bible is printed in Latin.

13585.q: Roughly how many Gutenberg Bibles still exist today?
13585.e: About 180 copies were printed. Around 50 survive today, some of them incomplete.
13585.m: Only around 50 Gutenberg Bibles exist today.

13586.q: What can you see in the Gutenberg Museum in Mainz?
13586.e: There is a Gutenberg Museum in Mainz. There you can see old printing presses and a Gutenberg Bible.
13586.m: At the Gutenberg Museum in Mainz you learn a lot about printing.

13587.q: How did the colourful pictures and first letters get into the Gutenberg Bible?
a: They were stuck on in gold foil
They were glued in from other books
13587.e: Only the black text was printed. Artists then painted the colourful decorations in by hand.
13587.m: The colours in the Gutenberg Bible were painted by hand.

13588.q: What did Gutenberg put together into words when printing?
a: Carved wooden blocks with whole pages
13588.e: Gutenberg cast single letters out of metal. He put this type together into words and lines and could use it again and again.
13588.m: Gutenberg printed with movable metal letters.

13589.q: Do we know exactly what Gutenberg looked like?
a: No, all pictures were made later
Yes, there is a statue from his time
13589.e: Nobody knows exactly what Gutenberg looked like. All pictures of him were made after his death.
13589.m: Nobody knows what Gutenberg really looked like.

13590.q: Why was printing faster than copying?
a: You could make many identical pages
13590.e: Once the letters were set, you could print the same page many times. A scribe had to copy every page one by one.
13590.m: Printing produced many identical pages quickly.

13591.q: Who is the university in Mainz named after?
13591.e: The university in Mainz is called Johannes Gutenberg University. That is how the city honours its famous inventor.
13591.m: Mainz University bears the name of Johannes Gutenberg.

13592.q: Which famous book did Gutenberg print?
13592.e: Gutenberg’s most famous work is the Bible. Its printing was finished in Mainz around 1455.
13592.m: Gutenberg’s most famous book is the Bible.

13593.q: Where does Johannes Gutenberg’s name come from?
a: From a house belonging to his family
From a mountain in the Alps
13593.e: The family lived in Mainz in the “Hof zum Gutenberg”. Johannes was named after this house.
13593.m: Gutenberg is named after a house in Mainz.

13594.q: On which river is Mainz, a river that also flows through Basel?
13594.e: Mainz is on the Rhine. The Rhine also flows through Basel and on to the North Sea.
13594.m: Mainz and Basel are both on the Rhine.

13595.q: Is Johannes Gutenberg a figure from legend, or did he really live?
13595.e: Gutenberg was a real person. There are old documents about him, and you can still see his Bibles today.

13596.e: The printers moved the press with their arms. They turned a large screw.
13596.m: Gutenberg’s press was worked by muscle power.

13597.q: On what were some Gutenberg Bibles printed to make them especially precious?
13597.e: Most Bibles were printed on paper. Some were printed on parchment, which is specially prepared animal skin.
13597.m: Some Gutenberg Bibles are printed on animal skin.

13598.q: How many volumes does a Gutenberg Bible usually have?
13598.e: The Bible has a great many pages. That is why it was usually bound in two thick volumes.
13598.m: A Gutenberg Bible usually consists of two thick volumes.

13599.q: In which year did Columbus reach America?
13599.e: On 12 October 1492, Columbus landed on an island in America. This year is very famous.

13600.q: Which city did Christopher Columbus come from?
13600.e: Columbus was born in Genoa. Genoa is a port city in what is now Italy.
13600.m: Columbus came from the port city of Genoa.

13601.q: For which country did Columbus sail in 1492?
13601.e: The Spanish king and queen paid for his voyage. That is why Columbus sailed for Spain.
13601.m: Columbus sailed on behalf of Spain.

13602.q: Where did Columbus actually want to sail to?
13602.e: Columbus wanted to sail west to reach India and Asia. He did not know that America lay in between.
13602.m: Columbus actually wanted to sail to India.

13603.q: With how many ships did Columbus set off on his first voyage?
13603.e: Columbus had one larger ship and two smaller, fast sailing ships with him.
13603.m: Columbus began his first voyage with three ships.

13604.q: What was the name of Columbus’s biggest ship?
13604.e: The Santa María was Columbus’s main ship. The other two were called Pinta and Niña.
13604.m: Columbus’s biggest ship was called the Santa María.

13605.q: What did Columbus call the people he met in America?
13605.e: Columbus thought he had arrived in Asia. That is why he called the people there “Indians”. The name stuck, even though it was wrong.
13605.m: Columbus mistakenly called the people in America Indians.

13606.e: Columbus sailed west from Spain across the Atlantic. America lies on the other side.
