23739.m: Horses are also part of the Terracotta Army.

23740.q: Who discovered the Terracotta Army in 1974?
23740.e: Farmers wanted to dig a well and came across pieces of clay figures. After that, large excavations began.
23740.m: Farmers found the Terracotta Army while digging a well.

23741.q: Roughly how many figures does the Terracotta Army have?
23741.e: Researchers estimate there are about 8000 soldiers. Many of them have not been dug up yet.
23741.m: The Terracotta Army has about 8000 figures.

23742.q: What do the faces of the clay soldiers look like?
23742.e: The craftsmen gave the soldiers different faces, hairstyles and beards. That is why almost every soldier looks different.
23742.m: Almost every clay soldier has a face of its own.

23743.q: What did the clay soldiers look like originally?
23743.e: The figures were originally painted in colours. Over time the paint has almost completely flaked off.
23743.m: The clay soldiers used to be brightly painted.

23744.q: Who is seen as the inventor of paper in China?
23744.e: Cai Lun was an official at the imperial court. Around AD 105 he improved the way paper was made so much that he is seen as its inventor.
23744.m: Cai Lun is seen as the inventor of paper.

23745.q: What was the first paper in China made from?
a: Plant fibres and scraps of cloth
23745.e: People boiled tree bark, hemp and old scraps of cloth into a pulp. Thin sheets were made from it.
23745.m: The first paper was made from plant fibres and scraps of cloth.

23746.q: What did people in China often write on before there was paper?
23746.e: People wrote on narrow strips of bamboo and tied them together. Such books were very heavy.
23746.m: Before paper, people in China wrote on bamboo.

23747.q: When making paper, what is used to scoop the fibre pulp out of the water?
23747.e: You dip a fine sieve into the fibre pulp and lift it out. The water drains away and a thin layer is left behind.
23747.m: Paper is scooped out of the fibre pulp with a sieve.

23748.q: What is the writing material of the ancient Egyptians, made from a marsh plant, called?
23748.e: Papyrus was made from the stems of a marsh plant. Our word “paper” comes from “papyrus”.
23748.m: The word “paper” comes from Egyptian papyrus.

23749.q: Who brought the art of papermaking from Asia to Europe?
23749.e: The Arabs learned how to make paper and brought it to Europe through Spain. Paper only arrived there in the Middle Ages.
23749.m: The Arabs brought paper to Europe.

23750.q: In which Swiss city is there a museum in an old paper mill?
23750.e: In Basel there is the Basel Paper Mill, a museum of paper, writing and printing. You can make your own paper there.
23750.m: At the Basel Paper Mill you can make paper yourself.

23751.q: Which animal makes the thread for silk?
23751.e: The silkworm spins a very fine thread. The fabric silk is woven from it.

23752.q: Which leaves does the silkworm like to eat most?
23752.e: Silkworms eat almost only the leaves of the mulberry tree. That is why many mulberry trees were planted.

23753.q: What does the silkworm spin around itself?
23753.e: The caterpillar wraps itself in a long thread. This makes a cocoon, from which the silk thread is unwound.
23753.m: The silkworm spins itself into a cocoon.

23754.q: What does a silkworm turn into if you let it hatch?
23754.e: The silkworm turns into a moth called the silk moth. It flies at night.
23754.m: The silkworm turns into a moth.

23755.q: How long can the thread of a single silk cocoon be?
23755.e: A cocoon is made of one single, very long thread. It can be several hundred metres long.
23755.m: A silk cocoon is made of one very long thread.

23756.q: According to a legend, a cocoon fell into a Chinese empress's cup. What was in it?
23756.e: The legend tells of Empress Leizu. In the hot tea the thread came loose from the cocoon, and so she discovered silk.
23756.m: According to the legend, silk was discovered in a cup of tea.

23757.q: For a long time, what was the making of silk in China?
23757.e: Anyone who gave away the secret of silk was severely punished. So only China could make silk and sell it at a high price.
23757.m: For a long time, silk making was a secret in China.

23758.q: Which Swiss city used to be famous for silk fabrics?
23758.e: In Zurich, silk fabrics were woven and traded for many centuries. Zurich's silk industry was once one of the largest in the world.
23758.m: Zurich used to be a famous silk city.

23759.e: The Silk Road was made up of many routes between China and the Mediterranean. Traders carried goods along them from place to place.
23759.m: The Silk Road was a network of trade routes.

23760.q: Between which areas did the Silk Road run?
23760.e: The trade routes ran from China right across Asia to the Mediterranean. There the precious silk was sold on.
23760.m: The Silk Road linked China with the Mediterranean.

23761.q: Which animals carried the goods through the deserts on the Silk Road?
23761.e: Camels can go a long time without water. That made them well suited for travelling through deserts.
23761.m: Camels carried the goods through the deserts.

23762.q: What do you call a group of traders travelling with camels?
23762.e: Traders travelled in caravans, which means in large groups. Together they were safer from robbers.
23762.m: A caravan is a travelling group with camels.

23763.q: Where did traders on the Silk Road stay overnight?
23763.e: A caravanserai was an inn with a courtyard for people and animals. Traders could sleep safely there.
23763.m: In a caravanserai, traders and camels found a place for the night.

23764.q: Did most traders travel the whole way from China to the Mediterranean?
a: No, the goods often changed hands
Yes, they all travelled the whole way
23764.e: Most traders only travelled part of the way. Then they sold the goods on to other traders.
23764.m: On the Silk Road, goods were passed from trader to trader.

23765.q: Apart from goods, what else was passed along the Silk Road?
23765.e: Knowledge, inventions and religions travelled with the traders. That is how Buddhism, for example, came to China.
23765.m: Ideas travelled along the Silk Road too.

23766.q: Which goods did traders from the West like to bring to China?
23766.e: The Chinese valued glass from the West. Silk, tea and paper, on the other hand, were made in China itself.
23766.m: Glassware travelled from the West to China.

23767.e: Qin Shi Huang united several kingdoms into one large empire. He was the first to call himself emperor.
23767.m: Qin Shi Huang was the first emperor of China.

23768.q: In which year did Qin Shi Huang become emperor?
23768.e: By 221 BC he had defeated all his rivals. After that he ruled all of China as emperor.
23768.m: Qin Shi Huang became emperor in 221 BC.

23769.q: What did Qin Shi Huang make the same throughout the empire?
23769.e: Before that, each kingdom had its own written characters, coins and measures. The emperor made them the same everywhere so that the empire held together better.
23769.m: The first emperor made writing, coins and measures the same everywhere.

23770.q: Roughly what does the title “Shi Huangdi” mean?
23770.e: “Shi” means first and “Huangdi” means emperor. He wanted many emperors to come after him.

23771.q: What did Qin Shi Huang search for during his life?
23771.e: The emperor was very afraid of death. He sent people out to find a potion for eternal life.
23771.m: Qin Shi Huang wanted to live for ever.

23772.q: What did Qin Shi Huang have built for the time after his death?
23772.e: While he was still alive he had work begin on a huge tomb. Many thousands of people worked on it.
23772.m: The first emperor had a huge tomb built for himself.

23773.q: What did Qin Shi Huang have burned because he would not tolerate other opinions?
23773.e: The emperor had many books burned that he did not like. Only books about medicine or farming were allowed to stay.
23773.m: The first emperor had many books burned.

23774.q: Which country's name probably comes from the state of Qin?
23774.e: “Qin” is pronounced roughly like “Chin”. Many researchers believe that the name China comes from it.
23774.m: The name China probably comes from the state of Qin.

23775.e: Confucius was a teacher who thought about how people should live together well. His teachings are still known today.
23775.m: Confucius was a famous teacher and thinker.

23776.e: Confucius lived from about 551 to 479 BC. That is about 2500 years ago.

23777.q: What does the Chinese name Kong Fuzi mean?
23777.e: “Fuzi” is a title of honour and means master. “Kong Fuzi” became “Confucius” in the West.

23778.q: What was especially important to Confucius?
a: Respect for parents and older people
23778.e: Confucius taught that children should honour their parents and respect older people. That way families would live together well.
23778.m: For Confucius, respect for parents and older people was very important.

a: Do not do to others what you would not want done to you
The early bird catches the worm
23779.e: Confucius said you should not do anything to others that you would not want yourself. This rule is also known from other religions.
23779.m: Do not do to others what you would not want done to you.

23780.q: Who wrote down the teachings of Confucius?
23780.e: Confucius's pupils wrote down his conversations and sayings. That is how they have survived until today.
23780.m: Confucius's pupils wrote down his teachings.

23781.q: According to Confucius, what should people do all their lives?
23781.e: Confucius thought learning was very important. He believed that people who learn become better people.
23781.m: Confucius said you should keep on learning.

23782.q: By what name is Siddhartha Gautama known?
23782.e: Siddhartha Gautama was later called Buddha. He is the founder of a major religion.
23782.m: Siddhartha Gautama is known as Buddha.

23783.e: Buddha means the awakened one. After a long search, Siddhartha had gained an important insight about life.

23784.q: What was Siddhartha Gautama before he became Buddha?
23784.e: Siddhartha was the son of a ruler and lived in a palace. There he had everything he wanted.
23784.m: Siddhartha Gautama was a prince at first.

23785.q: In which modern country was Siddhartha Gautama born?
23785.e: He was born in Lumbini. This place is in Nepal today, near the border with India.
23785.m: Buddha was born in today's Nepal.

23786.q: What did the young prince see for the first time outside the palace?
23786.e: In the palace, suffering had been kept away from him. Outside he saw old, sick and dead people and became very thoughtful.
23786.m: Outside, Siddhartha saw old age and illness for the first time.

23787.q: Under what kind of tree did Siddhartha awaken?
23787.e: The tree was a sacred fig. It is also called the Bodhi tree, which means tree of awakening.
23787.m: Buddha awakened under a fig tree.

23788.q: Which religion goes back to Siddhartha Gautama?
23788.e: Buddhism grew out of his teachings. Today Buddhists live all over the world, including in Switzerland.
23788.m: Buddhism goes back to Siddhartha Gautama.

23789.q: What are the famous colossal heads of the Olmecs?
23789.e: The Olmecs carved huge heads out of stone. Some are almost three metres high.
23789.m: The Olmecs made huge stone heads.

23790.q: In which modern country were the Olmec heads found?
23790.e: The Olmecs lived on the coast of the Gulf of Mexico. Their stone heads were found there.
23790.m: The Olmec heads come from Mexico.

23791.q: Roughly how big are the largest Olmec heads?
a: As tall as a church tower
23791.e: The largest stone heads are almost three metres high. That is taller than a room.
23791.m: The largest Olmec heads are almost three metres high.

23792.q: How heavy is a large Olmec head?
23792.e: The largest heads weigh many tonnes, as much as several cars put together. You cannot simply lift them.
23792.m: An Olmec head weighs several tonnes.

23793.q: Which rock are the Olmec heads carved from?
23793.e: The heads are made of basalt, a hard rock from volcanoes. The blocks came from mountains far away.
23793.m: The Olmec heads are made of volcanic rock.

23794.q: Who do the Olmec heads probably show?
23794.e: Researchers believe the heads show important rulers. Each head has its own facial features.
23794.m: The Olmec heads probably show rulers.

23795.q: Roughly how old are the Olmec heads?
23795.e: The Olmecs lived about 3000 years ago. They are one of the oldest advanced civilisations in the Americas.
23795.m: The Olmec heads are about 3000 years old.

23796.q: Roughly what does the name “Olmecs” mean?
23796.e: Rubber trees grew in their region. Rubber can be made from their sap.
23796.m: Olmecs means people from the rubber land.

23797.q: What shape are the pyramids of the Maya?
23797.e: Maya pyramids are step pyramids. A steep staircase leads to the top.

23798.q: What often stood at the very top of a Maya pyramid?
23798.e: A small temple stood at the top. Priests held ceremonies for the gods there.
23798.m: A temple often stood on top of Maya pyramids.

23799.q: What is the name of a famous Maya city with a large pyramid?
23799.e: Chichén Itzá is in Mexico. Machu Picchu, on the other hand, was built by the Incas in Peru.
23799.m: Chichén Itzá is a famous Maya city.

23800.q: In which part of the world did the Maya build their pyramids?
23800.e: The Maya lived in what is now Mexico, Guatemala and neighbouring countries. This region is called Central America.
23800.m: The Maya built their pyramids in Central America.

23801.q: The pyramid of Chichén Itzá has 4 staircases with 91 steps each and one more step at the top. How many steps is that?
23801.e: 4 times 91 is 364, and with the top step it makes 365. That is how many days a year has.
23801.m: The pyramid of Chichén Itzá has as many steps as the year has days.

23802.q: What can you see on the pyramid of Chichén Itzá in spring and autumn?
23802.e: On two days a year, the sun casts shadows on the staircase. It looks as if a snake is crawling down the pyramid.
23802.m: A shadow snake appears on the pyramid of Chichén Itzá.

23803.q: Where are many old Maya pyramids today?
23803.e: Many Maya cities were overgrown by the rainforest. Some pyramids are still being discovered in the jungle today.
23803.m: Many Maya pyramids are in the rainforest.

23804.q: Which game did the Maya play on courts next to their pyramids?
23804.e: The Maya built ball courts with high walls. The heavy rubber ball was not allowed to be touched with the hands.
23804.m: The Maya played a ball game on special courts.

23805.q: What value does a dot have in the Maya number system?
23805.e: The Maya wrote one as a dot. Two dots mean 2.
23805.m: For the Maya, a dot means one.

23806.q: What value does a bar have in the Maya number system?
23806.e: For the Maya, a horizontal bar means 5. It replaces five dots.
23806.m: For the Maya, a bar means five.

23807.q: How did the Maya write zero?
23807.e: For zero the Maya drew a sign that looks like a shell. Many other peoples did not yet know zero at that time.
23807.m: The Maya wrote zero as a shell.

23808.q: What number do three dots mean for the Maya?
23808.e: Each dot counts as 1. So three dots are 1 plus 1 plus 1, which makes 3.
23808.m: For the Maya, three dots mean three.

23809.q: For the Maya, a bar is 5 and a dot is 1. What number are two bars and one dot?
23809.e: Each bar is 5 and the dot is 1. So 5 plus 5 plus 1 makes 11.
23809.m: For the Maya, two bars and one dot make eleven.

23810.q: For the Maya, a bar is 5. What number are three bars?
23810.e: Each bar is 5. Three bars are 5 plus 5 plus 5, which makes 15.
23810.m: For the Maya, three bars mean fifteen.

23811.q: The Maya wrote a bar instead of five dots. So what is the most dots that can stand side by side?
23811.e: You do not write five dots, because there is a bar for that. So at most 4 dots stand side by side.
23811.m: With the Maya, at most four dots stand side by side.

23812.q: The Maya counted in groups of twenty. What is this probably connected with?
23812.e: A person has 10 fingers and 10 toes, 20 altogether. That made counting easy.
23812.m: The Maya probably counted to twenty with fingers and toes.

23813.q: How many days did the Maya solar year have?
23813.e: The Maya solar year is called the Haab. It had 365 days, almost like our year.
23813.m: The Maya solar year had 365 days.

23814.q: How many days did a month have in the Maya solar year?
23814.e: In the Maya solar year, each month had exactly 20 days. This fits their way of counting in twenties.
23814.m: A Maya month lasted twenty days.

23815.q: A Maya year had 18 months of 20 days each. How many days is that?
23815.e: 18 times 20 is 360 days. A few extra days were added at the end of the year.
23815.m: Eighteen months of twenty days each make 360 days.

23816.q: How were the five extra days at the end of the Maya year seen?
23816.e: The five days did not belong to any month. The Maya believed they brought bad luck.
23816.m: The last five days of the Maya year were seen as unlucky days.

23817.q: How many days did the sacred calendar of the Maya have?
23817.e: The sacred calendar is called the Tzolkin. It had 260 days and was used for festivals and rituals.
23817.m: The sacred calendar of the Maya had 260 days.

23818.q: After how many years did the two Maya calendars start on the same day again?
23818.e: Only after 52 years did both calendars meet again on the same starting day. This period is called the Calendar Round.
23818.m: A Maya Calendar Round lasted 52 years.

23819.q: Which planet did the Maya watch especially closely?
23819.e: Venus is very bright in the sky. The Maya calculated its movements very precisely and wrote them down in books.
23819.m: The Maya watched Venus very closely.

23820.q: What happened on 21 December 2012, when a long period of the Maya calendar ended?
23820.e: Some people believed the world would end on that day. But for the Maya, a new period of time simply began.
23820.m: When a Maya period of time ends, a new one simply begins.

23821.q: In which country are the Nazca Lines?
23821.e: The Nazca Lines are in a desert in the south of Peru. They are UNESCO World Heritage.
23821.m: The Nazca Lines are in Peru.

a: Huge pictures on the desert floor
23822.e: The lines are huge drawings on the desert floor. They show animals, plants and shapes.
23822.m: The Nazca Lines are huge pictures on the desert floor.

23823.q: Which bird is famous as a Nazca picture?
23823.e: The hummingbird is one of the best-known pictures in the Nazca desert. It is almost a hundred metres long.
23823.m: A huge hummingbird is drawn in the Nazca desert.

23824.q: From where can you see the Nazca pictures best?
23824.e: The pictures are so big that you can hardly make them out from the ground. From a plane you can see them well.
23824.m: You can see the Nazca pictures best from the air.

23825.q: How did the people of Nazca make the lines?
23825.e: The ground is covered with dark stones. Underneath is light sand, and that is how light lines appeared.
23825.m: Dark stones were cleared away to make the Nazca Lines.

23826.q: Why have the Nazca Lines survived until today?
a: Because it hardly ever rains there
Because they are made of concrete
Because they are under a roof
23826.e: The Nazca desert is one of the driest places on Earth. With no rain and little wind, the lines lasted a long time.
23826.m: The Nazca Lines survived in the dry desert.

23827.q: Roughly how old are the Nazca Lines?
23827.e: The Nazca culture drew the lines about 2000 years ago. That was roughly the time of the ancient Romans.
23827.m: The Nazca Lines are about 2000 years old.

23828.q: Which German researcher studied the Nazca Lines all her life?
23828.e: Maria Reiche measured the lines for decades and worked to protect them. She is greatly honoured in Peru.
23828.m: Maria Reiche devoted her life to the Nazca Lines.

23829.q: Who was the father of the hero Heracles?
23829.e: Heracles was a son of Zeus, the father of the gods, and the human woman Alcmene. That is why he was a demigod with enormous strength.
23829.m: Heracles was a son of Zeus.

23830.q: How many great tasks did Heracles have to complete?
23830.e: The legend tells of the twelve labours of Heracles. Each task was dangerous and seemed almost impossible.
23830.m: Heracles had to complete twelve tasks.

23831.q: Which animal did Heracles defeat near the city of Nemea?
23831.e: The Nemean lion had a hide that no weapon could pierce. Heracles strangled it and then wore its hide as a cloak.
23831.m: Heracles wore the hide of the Nemean lion.

23832.q: What happened if you cut off one of the Hydra's heads?
23832.e: The Hydra was a water serpent with many heads. For every head cut off, two new ones grew back, until the wounds were sealed with fire.
23832.m: For every head of the Hydra, two new ones grew back.

23833.q: Whose huge stables did Heracles have to clean out in a single day?
23833.e: King Augeas had a great many cattle, and his stables had not been cleaned for years. Heracles still managed it in one day.
23833.m: Heracles cleaned out the stables of Augeas.

23834.q: How did Heracles clean the stables of Augeas?
23834.e: Heracles diverted two rivers through the stables. The water washed all the dung out at once.
23834.m: Heracles let river water flow through the stables.

23835.q: Which dog did Heracles bring up from the underworld?
23835.e: Cerberus was a dog with three heads that guarded the entrance to the underworld. Heracles overpowered him with his bare hands.
23835.m: Cerberus guarded the underworld with three heads.

23836.q: What was Heracles called by the ancient Romans?
23836.e: The Romans took over many Greek legends. For them, Heracles became Hercules.

23837.q: What was the name of the six-headed monster that Odysseus had to sail past?
23837.e: Scylla lurked at a narrow strait and snatched sailors from the ships. On the other side a dangerous whirlpool threatened.
23837.m: Scylla was a monster with six heads.

23838.q: On which island was Odysseus king?
23838.e: Odysseus ruled the small Greek island of Ithaca. He wanted to return there after the war.

23839.q: What was the name of Odysseus's wife?
23839.e: Penelope waited faithfully for Odysseus for many years. She turned down all the men who wanted to marry her.

23840.q: What was the name of Odysseus's son?
23840.e: Telemachus was still a baby when his father went to war. When Odysseus came home, he was a young man.
23840.m: Telemachus is the son of Odysseus.

23841.q: How did Odysseus hear the song of the Sirens without following it?
a: He was tied to the mast
23841.e: The Sirens lured sailors to their doom with their singing. His companions had wax in their ears, and Odysseus had himself tied to the mast.
23841.m: Odysseus had himself tied to the mast.

23842.q: Into which animals did the sorceress Circe turn Odysseus's companions?
23842.e: Circe gave the men a magic potion, and they became pigs. Odysseus forced her to turn his companions back.
23842.m: Circe turned the companions into pigs.

23843.q: Which animal recognised Odysseus at once after 20 years?
23843.e: Odysseus came home disguised as a beggar, and nobody recognised him. Only his old dog Argos wagged his tail.

23844.q: With which nymph did Odysseus have to stay on an island for seven years?
23844.e: The nymph Calypso kept Odysseus on her island because she wanted to marry him. Only on the gods' orders did she let him sail on.
23844.m: Calypso kept Odysseus for seven years.

23845.q: How did Odysseus prove at home who he really was?
23845.e: Only Odysseus could string his old bow. He even shot the arrow through twelve axe holes.
23845.m: Only Odysseus could string his bow.

23846.q: What did the wind god Aeolus give Odysseus?
23846.e: The stormy winds were shut up in the bag. His curious companions opened it, and a storm drove the ship far away.
23846.m: Aeolus gave Odysseus a bag full of winds.

23847.q: What was the Trojan Horse made of?
23847.e: The Greeks built a huge horse out of wood. It was hollow inside.
23847.m: The Trojan Horse was made of wood.

23848.q: Who hid in the belly of the Trojan Horse?
23848.e: Greek fighters sat inside the hollow belly of the horse. The Trojans had no idea.
23848.m: Greek warriors hid inside the horse.

23849.q: Whose idea was the Trojan Horse?
23849.e: The cunning Odysseus came up with the trick of the wooden horse. That is how the Greeks got into the city.
23849.m: Odysseus came up with the trick of the wooden horse.

23850.q: Which city was tricked with the wooden horse?
23850.e: The Greeks besieged Troy for a long time without success. Only with the wooden horse did they manage to take the city.
23850.m: Troy was tricked with the wooden horse.

23851.q: What did the warriors do after climbing out of the wooden horse?
23851.e: The warriors crept to the gates and opened them from the inside. That way the whole Greek army could get into the city.
23851.m: The warriors opened the gates from the inside.

23852.q: Which king's daughter warned the Trojans, but nobody believed her?
23852.e: Cassandra could foretell the future. But a curse meant that nobody believed her.

23853.q: What did the Trojans do with the wooden horse?
a: They pulled it into the city
They threw it into the sea
They left it where it was
23853.e: The Trojans thought the horse was a gift to the gods. So they brought it through the gate themselves.
23853.m: The Trojans pulled the horse into the city themselves.

23854.q: What did the other Greeks do so that Troy would believe they had left?
23854.e: The Greek ships sailed off and hid behind an island. In the night they came back.
23854.m: The Greeks pretended to sail away.

23855.q: What grew on Medusa's head instead of hair?
23855.e: Medusa was a monster with living snakes on her head. They hissed and writhed.
23855.m: Medusa had snakes instead of hair.

23856.q: What happened to everyone who looked straight at Medusa?
23856.e: Medusa's gaze was so terrible that everyone turned to stone at once. That is why she was so feared.
23856.m: Anyone who looked at Medusa turned to stone.

23857.e: Perseus was sent out to fetch Medusa's head. With the help of the gods he succeeded.

23858.q: How did Perseus look at Medusa without turning to stone?
a: In the reflection of his shield
23858.e: Perseus only looked at the reflection in his shiny shield. That way he never looked at Medusa directly.
23858.m: Perseus only looked at Medusa's reflection.

23859.q: Which goddess helped Perseus in the fight against Medusa?
23859.e: Athena gave Perseus a highly polished shield. She liked to help clever heroes.

23860.q: Which group of monsters did Medusa belong to?
23860.e: Medusa was a Gorgon. That was the name for monsters with a terrible gaze.

23861.q: How many Gorgon sisters were there?
23861.e: There were three Gorgons: Stheno, Euryale and Medusa. Only Medusa was mortal.

23862.q: What did Perseus later use Medusa's head for?
a: He threw it into the sea
He buried it in the desert
23862.e: Even cut off, the head turned anyone who looked at it to stone. Perseus held it up to his enemies.
23862.m: Medusa's head could still turn people to stone later on.

23863.q: What kind of creature is Pegasus?
23863.e: Pegasus is a winged horse from the Greek legends. He could fly high through the air.
23863.m: Pegasus is a horse with wings.

23864.q: According to legend, from which monster did Pegasus spring?
23864.e: When Perseus cut off Medusa's head, Pegasus sprang out of her neck. That is how the legend tells it.

23865.e: Bellerophon tamed the winged horse. Together they had many adventures.

23866.q: Which monster did Bellerophon and Pegasus defeat?
23866.e: The Chimera was a fire-breathing monster, a mix of lion, goat and snake. Bellerophon attacked it from the air on Pegasus.
23866.m: Riding Pegasus, Bellerophon defeated the Chimera.

23867.q: What did Bellerophon use to tame Pegasus?
23867.e: The goddess Athena gave Bellerophon a golden bridle. With it, Pegasus could be ridden.

23868.q: What did Pegasus become at the end of the legend?
23868.e: Zeus placed Pegasus in the sky. There you can see him as the constellation Pegasus.
23868.m: Pegasus is a constellation in the sky today.

23869.q: According to legend, what appeared when Pegasus stamped his hoof on a mountain?
23869.e: With the stamp of his hoof, a spring bubbled up on Mount Helicon. It was called Hippocrene, the horse's spring.
23869.m: Pegasus's hoof made a spring bubble up.

23870.q: Where did Bellerophon, too full of himself, want to fly with Pegasus?
23870.e: Bellerophon wanted to ride up to the gods on Mount Olympus. So Zeus had Pegasus throw him off.
23870.m: Bellerophon wanted to go too high, up to Olympus.

23871.e: A labyrinth has many winding passages and dead ends. It is easy to get lost in it.

23872.q: Where was the Minotaur locked up?
23872.e: The Minotaur lived in a huge maze. Anyone who went in could not find the way out again.
23872.m: The Minotaur lived in the labyrinth.

23873.q: Which sail colour on Theseus's ship meant bad news?
23873.e: The ship had sailed to Crete with black sails. If he won, Theseus was to raise a light sail on the way home.
23873.m: A black sail meant bad news.

23874.q: Which king had the Minotaur locked up?
23874.e: King Minos of Crete had the monster hidden away. The name Minotaur means bull of Minos.
23874.m: King Minos locked up the Minotaur.

23875.q: How many young people had to be sent to the Minotaur each time?
a: A hundred boys and a hundred girls
23875.e: According to the legend, there were seven young men and seven young women. They were sent into the labyrinth as victims.
23875.m: Each time, fourteen young people had to go to the Minotaur.

23876.q: How did Theseus find his way out of the labyrinth?
a: With chalk marks on the walls
23876.e: Theseus tied a thread at the entrance and unwound it as he went. On the way back he simply followed the thread.
23876.m: A thread showed Theseus the way out.

23877.q: Who gave Theseus the thread that saved him?
23877.e: Ariadne was the daughter of King Minos. She fell in love with Theseus and helped him.

23878.q: From which city did young people have to be sent to the Minotaur?
23878.e: Athens regularly had to send young men and women to Crete. Theseus wanted to put an end to it.
23878.m: Athens had to send young people to Crete.

23879.q: According to legend, which sea is named after Theseus's father?
23879.e: On his way home, Theseus forgot to change the sail. His father Aegeus thought he was dead and threw himself into the sea, which has been called the Aegean ever since.
23879.m: The Aegean Sea is named after King Aegeus.

23880.q: What was the name of Icarus's father?
23880.e: Icarus was the son of the clever Daedalus. Together they wanted to escape.
23880.m: Daedalus was the father of Icarus.

23881.q: What did Daedalus make the wings from?
23881.e: Daedalus collected bird feathers. He stuck them together with wax to make large wings.
23881.m: The wings were made of feathers and wax.

23882.e: Icarus flew too close to the sun. The heat made the wax melt, and the feathers came loose.
23882.m: The sun made Icarus's wax melt.

23883.q: Where did Icarus fall when he crashed?
23883.e: The two of them were flying over the sea. Icarus fell into the waves.

23884.q: What did Daedalus advise his son before the flight?
a: Not too high, not too low
23884.e: Daedalus knew the dangers. Too high, the sun was too hot; too low, the feathers would get wet.
23884.m: Daedalus advised flying in the middle, between sun and sea.

23885.q: Why was Icarus not supposed to fly too low over the sea?
23885.e: The spray of the sea would have made the feathers wet and heavy. Then Icarus would not have been able to fly any more.
23885.m: Wet feathers are too heavy for flying.

23886.q: From which island did Daedalus and Icarus want to fly away?
23886.e: King Minos held Daedalus and his son on the island of Crete. Because the king had the ships guarded, the two escaped through the air.
23886.m: Daedalus and Icarus escaped from Crete.

23887.q: What does Icarus often stand for today when people tell his story?
23887.e: Icarus did not listen to his father and flew too high. So he stands for someone who recklessly dares too much.

23888.q: What was Poseidon the god of?
23888.e: Poseidon ruled over all the seas. He could stir up storms or calm the water.
23888.m: Poseidon was the god of the sea.

23889.e: A trident is a kind of spear with three points. It was Poseidon's symbol.

23890.q: Which god was Poseidon's brother and king of the gods?
23890.e: Zeus ruled over the sky and the gods. He and Poseidon were brothers.

23891.q: What is Poseidon called by the Romans?
23891.e: The Romans called the sea god Neptune. A planet is also named after him.

23892.q: Apart from the sea, Poseidon was also the god of which animals?
23892.e: Poseidon was also seen as the god of horses. He often rode in a chariot pulled by horses.
23892.m: Poseidon was also the god of horses.

23893.q: Apart from storms, which natural event could Poseidon cause?
23893.e: The Greeks believed Poseidon could shake the earth. That is why they also called him the Earthshaker.
23893.m: Poseidon could make the earth shake.

23894.q: According to legend, where did Poseidon live?
a: In a palace in the sea
In a cave in a mountain
23894.e: Poseidon had a magnificent palace deep down in the sea. From there he ruled over the water.
23894.m: Poseidon lived in a palace in the sea.

23895.q: Which brother of Poseidon ruled over the underworld?
23895.e: Zeus, Poseidon and Hades were brothers. Zeus ruled the sky, Poseidon the sea and Hades the underworld.
23895.m: Hades, Poseidon's brother, ruled the underworld.

23896.q: What was Athena the goddess of?
23896.e: Athena was the goddess of wisdom and of clever warfare. She often helped smart heroes.
23896.m: Athena was the goddess of wisdom.

23897.e: The owl was seen as a clever bird and was Athena's animal. That is why it is still a symbol of wisdom today.

23898.q: According to legend, with which god did Athena compete for the city of Athens?
23898.e: Athena and Poseidon both wanted to be the city's protecting god. Athena won, and the city is still called Athens today.
23898.m: Athena competed with Poseidon for Athens.

23899.q: What did Athena give the people of Athens?
23899.e: Athena and Poseidon competed for the city. The people liked Athena's gift, the olive tree, better.
23899.m: Athena gave Athens the olive tree.

23900.q: According to legend, where was Athena born from?
23900.e: Zeus had a terrible headache. Then Athena sprang out of his head.
23900.m: Athena sprang from the head of Zeus.

23901.q: What is Athena called by the Romans?
23901.e: The Romans worshipped the goddess of wisdom as Minerva. She had similar roles to Athena.

23902.q: Which weapon does Athena usually carry in pictures and statues?
23902.e: Athena is usually shown with a helmet and spear. This shows that she was also a goddess of war.

23903.q: Into which animal did Athena turn the weaver Arachne?
23903.e: Arachne boasted that she could weave better than Athena. As punishment, she had to keep weaving for ever as a spider.

23904.q: According to legend, who was Pandora?
23904.e: The gods created Pandora as the first woman. Each god gave her a special gift.
23904.m: According to legend, Pandora was the first woman.

23905.q: What was Pandora not allowed to do with the jar?
23905.e: Pandora was given a closed jar and told not to open it. But she was too curious.
23905.m: Pandora was not allowed to open the jar.

23906.q: What came out of Pandora's box?
a: All the evils of the world
23906.e: When Pandora lifted the lid, illness, hardship and suffering flew out. They have been in the world ever since.
23906.m: All the evils came out of the box.

23907.q: What was left behind in Pandora's box?
23907.e: Pandora quickly closed the lid again. Only hope was left inside.

23908.q: Which god sent Pandora to humans with the jar?
23908.e: The father of the gods wanted to punish humans. So he sent Pandora with the dangerous jar.

23909.q: Why did Zeus want to punish humans with Pandora?
a: They had lied to the gods
23909.e: Prometheus had stolen fire from the gods and brought it to humans. This made Zeus angry.

23910.q: In the oldest version of the story, what was Pandora's box?
23910.e: The poet Hesiod told of a large storage jar. Only much later did it become a box.
23910.m: The box was originally a jar.

23911.q: What do people mean today by “opening Pandora's box”?
23911.e: The expression means doing something that brings lots of problems with it. It goes back to the legend.
23911.m: If you open Pandora's box, you cause lots of trouble.

23912.q: In which famous poem is Achilles the main character?
23912.e: The Iliad tells of the anger of Achilles in the war over Troy. It is one of the oldest works of European poetry.
23912.m: The Iliad tells the story of Achilles.

23913.q: Why could Achilles hardly be wounded?
a: He was dipped in a magic river
He ate the food of the gods
23913.e: His mother dipped him as a baby in the river Styx in the underworld. She held him by the heel, which stayed dry.
23913.m: The water of the Styx made Achilles almost impossible to wound.

23914.q: Who was the mother of Achilles?
23914.e: Thetis was a nymph from the sea. She wanted to protect her son from death.
23914.m: Thetis was the mother of Achilles.

23915.q: Which Trojan hero did Achilles defeat?
23915.e: Hector was Troy's strongest fighter. Achilles defeated him in front of the city walls.

23916.q: Who hit Achilles with an arrow in his weak spot?
23916.e: The Trojan Paris shot an arrow. The god Apollo guided it straight to the heel.
23916.m: Paris hit Achilles with an arrow.

23917.q: What was the name of Achilles's best friend?
23917.e: Patroclus fought in Achilles's armour and fell in battle. Achilles was deeply sad and angry about it.

23918.q: Which part of our body is named after Achilles?
23918.e: The Achilles tendon connects the calf with the heel. It bears the hero's name.
23918.m: The Achilles tendon is named after Achilles.

23919.q: On which side did Achilles fight in the Trojan War?
23919.e: Achilles was the strongest warrior of the Greeks. Without him they had a hard time at Troy.

23920.q: What kind of creature was Chiron, the teacher of Achilles?
23920.e: Chiron was a centaur, which means half man and half horse. He was very wise and taught many heroes.
23920.m: The centaur Chiron was the teacher of Achilles.

23921.q: How many eyes did the Cyclops Polyphemus have?
23921.e: The Cyclopes were giants with only one eye in the middle of their forehead. Polyphemus was one of them.
23921.m: A Cyclops has only one eye.

23922.q: What kind of creature was Polyphemus?
23922.e: Polyphemus was a huge Cyclops. He lived as a shepherd on an island.

23923.q: Who was the father of Polyphemus?
23923.e: Polyphemus was a son of the sea god. That is why the sea god later took revenge on Odysseus.
23923.m: Polyphemus was a son of Poseidon.

23924.q: Where did Polyphemus keep Odysseus and his men prisoner?
23924.e: Polyphemus rolled a huge stone in front of the entrance. That way nobody could get out.
23924.m: Polyphemus locked the men in his cave.

23925.q: What name did Odysseus give Polyphemus?
23925.e: When Polyphemus called for help, he shouted: “Nobody is hurting me!” So none of the other Cyclopes came to help him.

23926.q: What did Odysseus give Polyphemus to drink?
23926.e: Odysseus gave the giant wine. Polyphemus drank a lot of it and fell fast asleep.
23926.m: Odysseus made Polyphemus sleepy with wine.

23927.q: What did Odysseus use to blind the Cyclops?
23927.e: Odysseus and his men heated a wooden stake in the fire until it glowed. They drove it into the Cyclops’s one eye.

23928.q: How did Odysseus and his men escape from the cave?
a: On the back of an eagle
23928.e: The blind Polyphemus only felt the backs of his sheep. The men clung on underneath their bellies.
23928.m: The men escaped clinging under the sheep.

23929.q: Which goddess was the Parthenon dedicated to?
23929.e: The Parthenon was the temple of the goddess Athena. She was the protector of the city of Athens.
23929.m: The Parthenon is the temple of the goddess Athena.

23930.q: What stone was the Parthenon built from?
23930.e: The Parthenon was built from pale marble. The marble came from a mountain near Athens.
23930.m: The Parthenon is built of white marble.

23931.q: Roughly how many years ago was the Parthenon built?
23931.e: The Parthenon was built from 447 to 432 BC. That is almost 2500 years ago.
23931.m: The Parthenon is almost 2500 years old.

23932.q: How many columns stand along the front of the Parthenon?
23932.e: Eight columns stand side by side along the narrow front of the Parthenon. Along each of the long sides there are 17 columns.
23932.m: There are eight columns at the front of the Parthenon.

23933.q: At the Erechtheion on the Acropolis, figures hold up the roof instead of columns. What do these figures show?
23933.e: At the Erechtheion, six figures of young women hold up the roof of a porch. They are called caryatids.
23933.m: At the Erechtheion, figures of women hold up the roof.

23934.q: Who played the women’s parts in ancient Greek theatre?
23934.e: In ancient Greek theatre only men were allowed on stage. Wearing masks, they also played the women’s parts.
23934.m: In Greek theatre only men acted.

23935.q: Where did the audience sit in a Greek theatre?
a: On stone steps on a hillside
In a hall with a roof
On wooden benches in a tent
23935.e: Greek theatres were built in the open air against a hillside. The audience sat on rows of stone seats rising in a semicircle.
23935.m: Greek theatres were in the open air on a hillside.

23936.q: What do you call a funny play?
23936.e: A comedy is a funny play that makes people laugh. The Greeks invented this kind of play.
23936.m: A comedy is a funny play.

23937.q: What do you call a serious, sad play?
23937.e: A tragedy is a serious play that usually ends sadly. Tragedies were already performed in ancient Athens.
23937.m: A tragedy is a sad play.

23938.q: Why can you hear very well even from the top row of the theatre at Epidaurus?
a: Because of the thick walls around it
Because of the wind from the sea
23938.e: The theatre at Epidaurus is built so cleverly that even quiet words can be heard in the top rows. There was no technology for this back then.
23938.m: At Epidaurus the theatre’s shape carries the sound to the top.

23939.q: What was the group called that sang and danced together in Greek theatre?
23939.e: Greek theatre had a chorus. It sang, danced and explained to the audience what was happening in the story.
23939.m: The chorus sang and danced in Greek theatre.

23940.e: An amphora is a large jar that was used to store and transport supplies.
23940.m: An amphora is a storage jar.

23941.q: How many handles does an amphora have?
23941.e: An amphora has two handles, one on each side. The word means roughly “carried on both sides”.

23942.q: What were amphorae usually made of?
23942.e: Amphorae were shaped from clay and then fired in a kiln.
23942.m: Amphorae are made of fired clay.

23943.q: What did the Greeks often transport in amphorae?
23943.e: Amphorae were used to transport liquids such as wine and olive oil, but also grain, for example on ships.
23943.m: Wine and olive oil travelled in amphorae.

23944.q: Why did many transport amphorae have a point at the bottom?
a: They could be pushed into sand
23944.e: With the point, amphorae could be pushed into sand or earth. On ships they could be stacked well this way.
23944.m: The point helped to stand amphorae up and stack them.

23945.q: What colours are many painted Greek vases?
23945.e: Many Greek vessels show black figures on reddish-brown clay or reddish-brown figures on a black background.
23945.m: Greek vases are often painted black and reddish brown.

23946.q: What did winners of contests in ancient Athens often receive as a prize?
23946.e: The winners received painted prize amphorae filled with olive oil. The oil was very valuable.
23946.m: Winners in Athens received amphorae of olive oil.

23947.q: How many main types of column did the ancient Greeks have?
23947.e: The Greeks built columns in three styles: Doric, Ionic and Corinthian.
23947.m: The Greeks had three types of column.

23948.q: Which Greek column has two scrolls at the top?
23948.e: You can recognise the Ionic column by the two spiral scrolls at its top.
23948.m: The Ionic column has scrolls at the top.

23949.q: Which Greek column is decorated with leaves at the top?
23949.e: The Corinthian column is decorated at the top with the leaves of a plant called acanthus. It is the most splendid of the Greek columns.
23949.m: The Corinthian column has leaves at the top.

23950.q: Which Greek column is the simplest and has no decoration at the top?
23950.e: The Doric column is plain and sturdy. At the top it only has a simple rounded band with a flat slab on it.
23950.m: The Doric column is the simplest.

23951.q: What kind of columns does the Parthenon in Athens mainly have?
23951.e: The Parthenon is surrounded on the outside by Doric columns. This suits its strong, plain appearance.

23952.q: What do Greek columns often have from top to bottom?
23952.e: Many Greek columns have vertical grooves. They are called flutes.
23952.m: Greek columns often have vertical grooves.

23953.q: What is the top part of a column called?
23953.e: The top part of a column is called the capital. It shows which type the column belongs to.
23953.m: The capital is the head of a column.

23954.q: What did the columns of Greek temples hold up?
23954.e: The columns stand all around the temple and carry the heavy roof with its stone beams.
23954.m: In Greek temples the columns hold up the roof.

23955.q: What is the last letter of the Greek alphabet?
23955.e: Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet. It is a long O.
23955.m: Omega is the last Greek letter.

23956.q: How many letters does the Greek alphabet have?
23956.e: The Greek alphabet has 24 letters. The English alphabet has 26 letters.

23957.q: Which Greek letter is also the name of the circle number 3.14?
23957.e: The circle number, about 3.14, is written with the Greek letter pi.
23957.m: The circle number is called pi.

23958.q: Which Greek letter looks like a triangle as a capital?
23958.e: Capital delta is written like a triangle. That is why triangular river mouths are also called deltas.
23958.m: Capital delta looks like a triangle.

23959.q: What is Archimedes said to have shouted when he had a good idea in the bath?
23959.e: According to legend, Archimedes shouted “Eureka!”. It is Greek and means “I have found it!”.

23960.q: On which island did Archimedes live?
23960.e: Archimedes lived in the city of Syracuse on the island of Sicily. Many Greeks lived there at that time.
23960.m: Archimedes lived in Syracuse on Sicily.

23961.q: With which simple tool did Archimedes want to move even the Earth?
23961.e: Archimedes studied the lever. He is said to have claimed that with a fixed point he could move the world.
23961.m: With a long lever you can lift heavy loads.

23962.q: What is the Archimedes screw used for?
23962.e: The Archimedes screw turns inside a tube and lifts water upwards. This way fields could be watered.
23962.m: The Archimedes screw moves water upwards.

23963.q: According to legend, what did Archimedes notice when he got into the bath?
23963.e: Archimedes saw that the water rose higher as he got into the tub. His body was pushing water aside.
23963.m: A body in water pushes water aside.

23964.q: What was Archimedes asked to check for the king of Syracuse?
a: Whether a crown was pure gold
Whether the city wall was strong enough
Whether a well had clean water
Whether a warship was fast enough
23964.e: The king wanted to know whether his crown was made of pure gold or whether cheaper silver had been mixed in.
23964.m: Archimedes tested the king’s golden crown.

23965.e: Archimedes was one of the greatest mathematicians of the ancient world. He also invented many machines.
23965.m: Archimedes was a great mathematician and inventor.

23966.q: Roughly how many years ago did Archimedes live?
23966.e: Archimedes lived from about 287 to 212 BC. That is about 2200 years ago.

23967.e: Pythagoras was born on the Greek island of Samos. He lived about 2500 years ago.

23968.q: Which triangles does Pythagoras’ theorem apply to?
23968.e: Pythagoras’ theorem only applies to triangles with a right angle, that is a corner like the corner of a sheet of paper.
23968.m: Pythagoras’ theorem applies to right-angled triangles.

23969.q: In which region did Pythagoras found his school?
23969.e: Pythagoras moved to Croton in southern Italy. There he founded a community of pupils.

23970.q: What did Pythagoras and his pupils think was the origin of everything?
23970.e: Pythagoras and his pupils believed that the whole world could be explained with numbers.

23971.q: Which three numbers are a famous example of Pythagoras’ theorem?
23971.e: A triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 has a right angle, because 3 times 3 plus 4 times 4 is 25, and that is 5 times 5.
23971.m: A triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 has a right angle.

23972.q: Besides numbers, what else did Pythagoras study?
23972.e: Pythagoras is said to have discovered that pleasant harmonies are linked to simple number ratios, for example in the length of strings.
23972.m: Pythagoras studied the numbers in music.

23973.q: Roughly how many years ago did Pythagoras live?
23973.e: Pythagoras lived from about 570 BC until after 510 BC. That is about 2500 years ago.

23974.q: In which language did Homer compose his poems?
23974.e: Homer composed in an old form of Greek. His works are still read in many schools today.
23974.m: Homer wrote his poems in Greek.

23975.q: What else does the word “odyssey” mean today?
23975.e: Because Odysseus wandered for so long, any long, difficult journey is called an odyssey today.
23975.m: An odyssey is a long, wandering journey.

23976.q: How were Homer’s stories first passed on?
23976.e: Singers performed the long poems from memory. Only later were they written down.
23976.m: Homer’s stories were first sung and told.

23977.q: What is known about Homer’s birthplace?
23977.e: Several places claimed that Homer came from there, for example Smyrna and the island of Chios. Nobody knows for sure even today.

23978.q: How have people often imagined Homer since ancient times?
23978.e: Even in ancient times people said that Homer was a blind singer. Whether this is true is not known for certain.
23978.m: Homer is often shown as a blind singer.

23979.q: Roughly how many years ago were Homer’s works created?
23979.e: Experts think that Homer’s works were created in about the 8th or 7th century BC. That is about 2700 years ago.
23979.m: Homer’s works are about 2700 years old.

23980.q: How long is a marathon today?
23980.e: Since 1921 a marathon has been exactly 42.195 kilometres long.

23981.q: Where does the marathon get its name from?
23981.e: Marathon is a place in Greece, north-east of Athens. A famous battle took place there long ago.
23981.m: The marathon is named after the place Marathon.

23982.q: In the Marathon legend, what is the runner said to have announced in Athens?
23982.e: According to legend, a messenger ran from Marathon to Athens to announce the victory. Afterwards he is said to have collapsed, exhausted.
23982.m: The Marathon messenger brought news of the victory to Athens.

23983.q: Roughly how many years ago was the Battle of Marathon?
23983.e: The Battle of Marathon was in 490 BC. That is about 2500 years ago.
23983.m: The Battle of Marathon was about 2500 years ago.

23984.q: What is the runner from the Marathon legend usually called?
23984.e: The messenger in the legend is usually called Pheidippides. Whether he really ran from Marathon to Athens is not certain.
23984.m: The runner in the Marathon legend is usually called Pheidippides.

23985.q: Roughly how long is a half marathon?
23985.e: A half marathon is half as long as a marathon, so about 21.1 kilometres.
23985.m: A half marathon is about 21 kilometres long.

23986.q: What did pupils in ancient Athens often write on?
23986.e: The pupils scratched letters into a wooden tablet covered with wax. Afterwards the wax could be smoothed out again.
23986.m: Greek pupils wrote on wax tablets.

23987.q: What did pupils in ancient Athens use to write in the wax of their tablets?
23987.e: A pointed stylus was used to scratch the letters into the wax. The flat other end could smooth them away again.
23987.m: People wrote in wax with a stylus.

23988.q: What was the servant called who took a boy to school in Athens?
23988.e: A paedagogus was a slave who took the boy to school and looked after him. Today the related word “pedagogue” means a teacher.
23988.m: The paedagogus took the boy to school.

23989.q: Which musical instrument did pupils in Athens often learn to play?
23989.e: Music was part of lessons. The boys learned to play the lyre and to sing along.
23989.m: Pupils in Athens learned to play the lyre.

23990.q: What was the place called where young Greeks did sport?
23990.e: In the gymnasion, young men trained in running, wrestling and throwing. Our word “gymnasium” comes from this word.
23990.m: Young Greeks did sport in the gymnasion.

23991.q: What did most girls in ancient Athens learn at home?
23991.e: Most girls did not go to school. At home they learned spinning, weaving and housekeeping from their mother.
23991.m: Girls in Athens learned spinning and weaving at home.

23992.e: A trireme was a fast Greek warship that was powered mainly by rowers.
23992.m: A trireme is a Greek warship with oars.

23993.q: In how many rows, one above the other, did the rowers of a trireme sit?
23993.e: The rowers sat in three rows, one above the other. The name comes from the word for three.
23993.m: In a trireme, three rows of rowers sat one above the other.

23994.q: What did a trireme have at the front, just below the water?
23994.e: At the front the trireme had a bronze ram. It used it to ram enemy ships and smash holes in them.
23994.m: The trireme rammed other ships with its ram.

23995.q: Roughly how many rowers did a trireme have?
23995.e: A trireme had about 170 rowers. On top of that there were sailors, soldiers and the captain.

23996.q: Apart from oars, what did a trireme use to move?
23996.e: When the wind was good, the trireme could set sails. In battle, however, it used only oars.

23997.q: Who usually rowed the triremes of Athens?
23997.e: The rowers of the Athenian fleet were mostly free citizens who had little money. They were paid for their work.
23997.m: In Athens the rowers were mostly free citizens.

23998.q: Which god was the Oracle of Delphi dedicated to?
23998.e: A large temple of the god Apollo stood at Delphi. Apollo was believed to speak to people through the oracle.
23998.m: The Oracle of Delphi belonged to the god Apollo.

23999.q: What was the priestess called who gave the answers at Delphi?
23999.e: The priestess at Delphi was called the Pythia. She told people the answers of the god.
23999.m: The priestess of Delphi was called the Pythia.

24000.q: What did the ancient Greeks believe about Delphi?
a: That it was the centre of the world
That it was the coldest place
That it lay under the sea
That it was the oldest harbour
24000.e: The Greeks thought Delphi was the navel of the world. A special stone called the omphalos marked this centre.
24000.m: Delphi was seen as the navel of the world.

24001.q: Which saying was written on the temple at Delphi?
24001.e: The saying “Know yourself” was written on the temple of Apollo at Delphi. It is still famous today.

24002.q: What were the answers of the Oracle of Delphi often like?
24002.e: The oracle’s answers were often like riddles. They could be understood in different ways.
24002.m: The oracle often gave puzzling answers.

24003.e: Delphi lies on a steep slope of the Parnassus mountains in central Greece.

24004.e: Olympus is a mountain range in the north of Greece. Its highest peak is the highest point in the country.
24004.m: Olympus is the highest mountain in Greece.

24005.q: Roughly how high is Mount Olympus?
24005.e: The highest peak of Olympus is about 2918 metres high. That is about 400 metres more than the Säntis in eastern Switzerland.

24006.q: According to legend, what did the gods on Olympus eat?
24006.e: The gods ate ambrosia. This food was meant to keep them immortal.
24006.m: The food of the gods is called ambrosia.

24007.q: Since 1987 the Acropolis has been on a special list. Which one?
a: The Seven Wonders of the World
24007.e: The Acropolis of Athens has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987. Such places are meant to be protected for everyone.
24007.m: The Acropolis is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

24008.q: What did the figures on the Parthenon look like in the past?
24008.e: The figures and decorations on the Parthenon used to be brightly painted. Over time the colours have almost completely disappeared.
24008.m: Greek temple figures used to be brightly painted.

24009.q: In which museum outside Greece are many figures from the Parthenon today?
a: The Swiss National Museum in Zurich
24009.e: Around 1800 an Englishman called Lord Elgin had many figures from the Parthenon taken to England. Today they are in the British Museum, and Greece would like them back.
24009.m: Many Parthenon figures are now in London.

24010.q: What was the round area in front of the stage where the chorus danced called?
24010.e: The round dancing area in a Greek theatre was called the orchestra. Our word “orchestra” comes from it.
24010.m: The chorus danced in the orchestra.

24011.q: Roughly how many spectators could the theatre at Epidaurus hold?
24011.e: After it was enlarged, the theatre at Epidaurus held up to about 14,000 people. It is still used for performances today.
24011.m: Over 10,000 people sat in the theatre at Epidaurus.

24012.q: In which direction is Greek written today?
24012.e: Today Greek is written from left to right, like English. In very ancient times it was sometimes written the other way round too.
24012.m: Greek is written from left to right.

24013.q: Which sounds did the Greeks write with their own letters, which many older scripts did not?
24013.e: The Greeks also wrote vowels such as A, E and O with their own letters. This made words much easier to read.
24013.m: The Greeks also wrote down the vowels.

24014.q: Which small Greek letter looks a bit like a w?
24014.e: Small omega is written like a rounded w: ω. Even so, it is pronounced like a long O.
24014.m: Small omega looks like a w.

24015.q: Which two famous works are credited to the poet Homer?
a: The Iliad and the Epic of Gilgamesh
24015.e: The Iliad tells of the Trojan War, the Odyssey of the long journey home of Odysseus. Both are considered works of Homer.
24015.m: The Iliad and the Odyssey are credited to Homer.

24016.q: Which war does Homer’s Iliad tell of?
24016.e: The Iliad tells of part of the war of the Greeks against Troy. Ilion is another name for Troy.
24016.m: The Iliad tells of the Trojan War.

24017.q: Roughly how far is it from Marathon to Athens?
24017.e: It is about 40 kilometres from Marathon to Athens. That is why a marathon today is over 40 kilometres long.
24017.m: Marathon is about 40 kilometres from Athens.

24018.q: What do you call a race that is even longer than a marathon?
24018.e: An ultramarathon is any race longer than a marathon. Some are over 100 kilometres.
24018.m: An ultramarathon is longer than a marathon.

24019.q: At about what age did boys in Athens start school?
24019.e: Boys from citizen families started learning with a teacher at about seven. That is similar to us today.
24019.m: Boys in Athens started school at about seven.

24020.q: What did the Greek word that our word “school” comes from mean?
24020.e: The Greek word “scholē” means free time. Only people who had time and did not have to work could learn.
24020.m: “School” comes from the Greek word for free time.

24021.q: What was a trireme mainly built from?
24021.e: Triremes were built of wood, which made them light and fast. Only the ram at the front was made of metal.
24021.m: Triremes were light ships made of wood.

24022.q: What did the Pythia sit on when she made prophecies?
24022.e: The Pythia sat on a tall stool with three legs, a tripod. She is shown like this on old vases too.
24022.m: The Pythia sat on a tripod.

24023.q: In which part of Greece is Mount Olympus?
24023.e: Mount Olympus is in the north of Greece, not far from the sea, between the regions of Thessaly and Macedonia.
24023.m: Olympus is in the north of Greece.

24024.q: According to legend, what did the gods on Olympus drink?
24024.e: According to legend, the gods drank nectar. Like their food, it was meant to keep them young for ever.
24024.m: The drink of the gods is called nectar.

24025.q: According to legend, how many great gods lived on Olympus?
24025.e: The Greeks told of twelve great gods on Olympus. Their king was Zeus.
24025.m: Twelve great gods lived on Olympus.

24026.q: What has the area around Mount Olympus been since 1938?
24026.e: In 1938 the area around Olympus became Greece’s first national park. Plants and animals are protected there.
24026.m: Greece’s first national park is at Olympus.

24027.q: Which shape does the famous Pythagoras’ theorem apply to?
24027.e: Pythagoras’ theorem applies to triangles with a right angle. It is named after Pythagoras but was known even earlier.
24027.m: Pythagoras’ theorem applies to right-angled triangles.

24028.q: An amphora is a large clay jar. Who made jars like this?
24028.e: Amphorae were shaped by potters on a potter’s wheel and then fired.

24029.q: What were the thermae in ancient Rome?
24029.e: The thermae were public baths. Many Romans bathed there almost every day.
24029.m: The thermae were the Romans’ large bathhouses.

24030.q: What was the hot room in the Roman baths called?
24030.e: In the caldarium the water was hot and the air was warm and damp. The word comes from the Latin “calidus”, meaning hot.
24030.m: The caldarium was the hottest room in the baths.

24031.q: What was there in the frigidarium of the baths?
24031.e: The frigidarium was the cold room. People cooled down there after their warm bath.
24031.m: In the frigidarium people bathed in cold water.

24032.q: What was the lukewarm room between hot and cold called?
24032.e: In the tepidarium it was pleasantly lukewarm. This way the body slowly got used to the heat.
24032.m: The tepidarium was the lukewarm room of the baths.

24033.q: What did the Romans use in the baths to scrape oil and dirt off their skin?
24033.e: The Romans hardly knew soap. They rubbed themselves with oil and scraped it off again with a curved scraper called a strigil.
24033.m: The Romans cleaned themselves with oil and a scraper.

24034.q: What else could you do at the baths besides bathing?
24034.e: Many baths had a sports ground. People also met friends there and shared the latest news.
24034.m: The baths were also a meeting place for sport and chatting.

24035.q: In which Swiss town did even the Romans bathe in hot springs?
24035.e: In Baden in the canton of Aargau, warm water bubbles out of the ground. The Romans called the place Aquae Helveticae and built baths there.
24035.m: Even the Romans bathed in the warm water at Baden.

24036.q: What did most people have to pay to get into the baths?
a: Nothing, only slaves had to pay
24036.e: Entry to the public baths was very cheap. That way even poor people could go bathing.
24036.m: Almost all Romans could afford the baths.

24037.q: Who fought in front of the spectators in the Colosseum?
24037.e: Gladiators were fighters who fought each other to entertain the crowd. Many of them were slaves.

24038.q: What shape is the Colosseum, seen from above?
24038.e: The Colosseum is an amphitheatre. It has the shape of an oval, which is a stretched-out circle.

24039.q: What was under the floor of the arena in the Colosseum?
24039.e: Under the arena there was a network of passages and rooms. Animals and fighters waited there until lifts brought them up.
24039.m: Passages and cages lay under the arena of the Colosseum.

24040.q: Which animals, among others, were shown in the Colosseum?
24040.e: For the animal hunts, wild animals were brought to Rome from many countries. Lions came from Africa, for example.
24040.m: Wild animals such as lions were also shown in the Colosseum.

24041.q: What was stretched over the Colosseum to keep off the sun?
24041.e: Sailors used masts to stretch a giant cloth over the seating. It was called the velarium and gave shade.
24041.m: A huge awning protected the spectators in the Colosseum from the sun.

24042.q: Roughly when was the Colosseum opened?
24042.e: The Colosseum opened in AD 80. That is almost 2000 years ago.
24042.m: The Colosseum is almost 2000 years old.

24043.q: How many storeys does the outer wall of the Colosseum have?
24043.e: The outer wall has three storeys of arches with a fourth, closed storey on top. It is almost 50 metres high.
24043.m: The outer wall of the Colosseum has four storeys.

24044.q: What did the winner of a chariot race receive as a sign of victory?
24044.e: For the Romans the palm branch was a sign of victory. Successful charioteers also often received a lot of money.
24044.m: The winner of a chariot race received a palm branch.

24045.q: Which animals pulled the racing chariots in the Circus Maximus?
24045.e: The light racing chariots were pulled by fast horses. The charioteers stood on the chariot.
24045.m: Horses pulled the Romans’ racing chariots.

24046.q: How many horses pulled a quadriga?
24046.e: The word quadriga comes from the Latin word for four. A quadriga is a chariot with four horses side by side.

24047.q: How many laps did a race in the Circus Maximus usually have?
24047.e: A race usually lasted seven laps. The laps were counted with figures that were turned round or taken down after each lap.
24047.m: A chariot race usually had seven laps.

24048.q: How could you tell the racing teams in the Circus Maximus apart?
a: By the shape of their chariots
24048.e: There were four teams: the Reds, the Whites, the Blues and the Greens. The fans supported their colour, just like in football today.
24048.m: The racing teams in Rome were recognised by their colours.

24049.q: What separated the two sides of the racetrack in the middle?
24049.e: In the middle of the track there was a long wall with statues and columns. The chariots raced around this wall.
24049.m: The chariots raced around a long wall in the middle.

24050.q: Why were the bends particularly dangerous in a chariot race?
a: The ground there was made of stone
Spectators sat on the track there
24050.e: On the tight bends, chariots often crashed into each other or overturned. Such accidents were feared.
24050.m: The tight bends were dangerous in a chariot race.

24051.q: What is the Circus Maximus today?
24051.e: Almost nothing is left of the stands. Today you can see a long grassy field in Rome in the shape of the old racetrack.
24051.m: The Circus Maximus is now a long grassy field in Rome.

24052.q: Which number is the Roman XX?
24052.e: X stands for ten. Two Xs make 10 + 10, which is 20.

24053.q: How do you write the number 3 in Roman numerals?
24053.e: You write the sign I for one three times. 1 + 1 + 1 makes 3.
24053.m: The number three in Roman numerals is III.

24054.q: Which number is the Roman IV?
24054.e: If the smaller sign I comes before the V, you subtract. 5 minus 1 makes 4.

24055.q: Which number is the Roman XII?
24055.e: X is ten and II is two. 10 + 2 makes 12.

24056.e: C stands for a hundred. That fits the Latin word “centum”, meaning a hundred.
24056.m: The Roman C means a hundred.

24057.e: M stands for a thousand. The Latin word for it is “mille”.
24057.m: The Roman M means a thousand.

24058.q: Which number is missing from Roman numerals?
24058.e: The Romans had no sign for zero. This number only came to Europe much later, from India via the Arab world.
24058.m: The Romans had no sign for zero.

24059.q: What does the Latin word “terra” mean?
24059.e: “Terra” means earth or land. The word “terrace” comes from it, for example.

24060.q: What does the Latin word “aqua” mean?
24060.e: “Aqua” means water. Words like aquarium and aquatic come from it.

24061.q: What does the Latin greeting “Salve” mean?
24061.e: The Romans greeted each other with “Salve”. It means something like “Be well” or “Greetings”.
24061.m: The Romans greeted each other with “Salve”.

24062.q: What does the car country code CH stand for?
24062.e: CH is the abbreviation of the Latin name for Switzerland. It means Swiss Confederation.
24062.m: CH stands for the Latin name Confoederatio Helvetica.

24064.q: Which script do we use today that the Romans already had?
24064.e: Our letters A, B, C and so on come from the Romans. We call them the Latin alphabet.
24064.m: Our letters come from the Romans.

24065.q: What does the Latin word “mater” mean?
24065.e: “Mater” means mother. You can hear how similar it is to the English word.

24066.q: What does the Latin word “rex” mean?
24066.e: “Rex” means king. In its earliest times, Rome was ruled by kings.

24067.e: The toga was a long cloth made of wool. It was wrapped skilfully around the body.
24067.m: The toga was a large cloth made of wool.

24068.q: Who was allowed to wear a toga in ancient Rome?
24068.e: The toga was the dress of Roman citizens. Slaves and foreigners were not allowed to wear it.
24068.m: The toga showed that someone was a Roman citizen.

24069.q: What colour was the ordinary toga?
24069.e: The normal toga was white or had the pale colour of undyed wool.

24070.q: What did a Roman wear under the toga?
24070.e: The tunic was a simple shirt-like garment. Many people wore only a tunic for work.
24070.m: A tunic was worn under the toga.

24071.q: What did the toga of boys and high officials have along its edge?
24071.e: This toga was called the toga praetexta. Its edge was decorated with a reddish-purple stripe.
24071.m: Boys wore a toga with a purple stripe.

24072.q: Why did people often need help putting on a toga?
24072.e: The toga was several metres long. So that it fell in nice folds, a slave often helped to drape it.
24072.m: The long toga was hard to put on.

24073.q: What did married Roman women wear instead of a toga?
24073.e: Married Roman women wore a long dress called a stola. They often put a cloak over it.

24074.q: Which modern word comes from the white toga worn by people seeking office?
24074.e: Anyone standing for an office wore a specially white toga. The Latin word “candidus” means shining white.
24074.m: The word candidate comes from the white toga.

24075.q: What was an insula in ancient Rome?
24075.e: An insula was a block of flats with several storeys. Many families lived in it and paid rent.
24075.m: An insula was a Roman block of flats.

24076.q: What does the Latin word “insula” actually mean?
24076.e: “Insula” means island. A block of flats was surrounded by streets, like an island by water.

24077.q: What was on the ground floor of many insulae?
24077.e: Downstairs, facing the street, there were small shops, snack bars and workshops. The flats were above them.
24077.m: There were often shops on the ground floor of an insula.

24078.q: Who usually lived right at the top of an insula?
24078.e: The upper floors were cramped and cheap. People with little money lived there.
24078.m: The poorer people lived right at the top of the insula.

24079.q: Which danger was especially common in the insulae?
24079.e: The houses were partly built of wood and people cooked over open fires. That is why fires broke out often.
24079.m: Fires often broke out in Rome’s blocks of flats.

24080.q: Where did people on the upper floors get their water from?
a: From the fountain in the street
From a pipe in the flat
From a well in the cellar
From a tank on the roof
24080.e: There was no running water upstairs. People carried water up in jugs from the public fountain.
24080.m: In an insula you had to fetch water from the fountain.

24081.q: Why did Emperor Augustus set a maximum height for insulae?
a: Because the temples were meant to be taller
Because the emperor wanted the view
24081.e: Some blocks of flats were badly built and collapsed. So Augustus only allowed buildings up to about 20 metres high.
24081.m: Augustus limited the height of blocks of flats.

24082.q: Where did many residents of an insula go to the toilet?
a: To the cellar of the insula
24082.e: Most flats had no toilet. People went to public latrines, where many sat side by side.

24083.q: Who lived in a Roman villa in the countryside?
24083.e: A villa was a large country house. It belonged to rich families and often had a farm with it.
24083.m: Rich Romans lived in a villa.

24084.q: Where did the Romans usually lay their mosaics?
24084.e: Many mosaics decorated the floors of villas and baths. They last a very long time.
24084.m: The Romans often laid mosaics on the floor.

24085.q: A famous picture made of tiny stones in Pompeii shows a dog. What is written with it?
24085.e: In Latin it says “Cave canem”. The picture shows a dog on a chain.

24086.q: What was the atrium in a Roman house?
24086.e: The atrium was a large hall behind the entrance. There was an opening in the roof that let in light and rain.
24086.m: The atrium was the entrance hall of a Roman house.

24087.q: What was the pool in the middle of the atrium for?
24087.e: Rain fell through the opening in the roof into the pool. The water was collected and used.
24087.m: In the atrium a pool collected rainwater.

24088.q: What was the peristyle in a villa?
24088.e: The peristyle was a garden inside the house. A walkway with columns ran all around it.
24088.m: The peristyle was a garden surrounded by columns.

24089.q: In which Swiss town can you see large Roman mosaics from a villa?
24089.e: Near Orbe in the canton of Vaud, the remains of a large Roman villa were found. Its beautiful mosaics can still be seen today.
24089.m: You can see Roman mosaics in Orbe.

24090.e: The Forum Romanum was the most important square in the city of Rome. People met there, traded and listened to speeches.
24090.m: The Forum Romanum was the main square of Rome.

24091.q: What, among other things, did people do in the Forum Romanum?
24091.e: The Forum had markets, shops and law courts. Politicians gave speeches to the people there.
24091.m: In the Forum people traded and talked.

24092.q: Which buildings stood in the Forum Romanum?
24092.e: Several temples to the Roman gods stood in the Forum, for example one to Saturn.
24092.m: Temples to the gods stood in the Forum Romanum.

24093.q: Where did the Senate meet in the Forum?
24093.e: The Curia was the senators’ meeting house. The building still stands in the Forum today.
24093.m: The Senate met in the Curia.

24094.q: What did the Vestal Virgins have to guard in the Temple of Vesta?
24094.e: The Vestal Virgins were priestesses. They made sure that the sacred fire of the goddess Vesta never went out.
24094.m: The Vestal Virgins guarded the sacred fire.

24095.q: What is a triumphal arch, like the one in the Forum?
24095.e: Triumphal arches were built for victorious generals and emperors. In the Forum, for example, there is the Arch of Titus.
24095.m: A triumphal arch commemorates a victory.

24096.q: What can you see of the Forum Romanum in Rome today?
a: Old columns and remains of walls
24096.e: What is left of the buildings is mainly columns and remains of walls. Today tourists from all over the world visit these ruins.
24096.m: The Forum Romanum is full of ruins today.

24097.q: What was the famous road through the Forum Romanum called?
24097.e: Via Sacra means “Sacred Way”. Triumphal processions passed along it through the Forum.
24097.m: The Via Sacra ran through the Forum Romanum.

24098.e: The hypocaust heated rooms from below. Warm air flowed underneath the floor.
24098.m: The hypocaust was Roman underfloor heating.

24099.q: What was used to make the fire for the hypocaust?
24099.e: Wood was burnt in a furnace outside the room. The hot air then flowed under the floor.
24099.m: The Romans heated the hypocaust with wood.

24100.q: What did the floor above the hypocaust stand on?
24100.e: The floor rested on many small pillars made of bricks. In between there was room for the warm air.
24100.m: In a hypocaust the floor stood on small pillars.

24101.q: After the floor, where else did the warm air flow through?
24101.e: Hollow tiles in the walls carried the warm air upwards. So the walls became warm too.
24101.m: With a hypocaust the walls became warm too.

24102.q: Who usually had to stoke the fire for the hypocaust?
24102.e: The fire had to burn for a long time and be fed with wood all the time. This hard work was usually done by slaves.
24102.m: Slaves kept the fire in the furnace burning.

24103.q: Which buildings often had a hypocaust?
24103.e: The heating was expensive. It was mainly built into baths and the houses of rich people.
24103.m: Baths and villas often had underfloor heating.

24104.q: What does the word hypocaust roughly mean?
24104.e: The word comes from Greek. “Hypo” means under and “kaiein” means to burn or heat.

24105.q: How did rich Romans eat at a banquet?
24105.e: At a fine meal the guests lay on wide couches. This was considered elegant.
24105.m: Rich Romans ate lying down at a banquet.

24106.q: Which side did the guests usually lie on while eating?
24106.e: The guests leaned on their left elbow. That left their right hand free for eating.
24106.m: At a banquet people leaned on their left arm.

24107.q: What did the Romans mainly eat with?
24107.e: The Romans ate a lot with their fingers. There were spoons and knives, but hardly any forks for eating.
24107.m: The Romans mostly ate with their fingers.

24108.q: How many couches usually stood around the table in the dining room?
24108.e: The dining room was called the triclinium. The word means that three couches stood around a table.
24108.m: Three couches stood in the triclinium.

24109.q: Which salty fish sauce did the Romans love?
24109.e: Garum was a salty sauce made from fermented fish. Mulsum was honeyed wine, posca a vinegar drink and puls a porridge.
24109.m: The Romans liked to season food with the fish sauce garum.

24110.q: Who brought the food at a rich family’s banquet?
24110.e: In rich families, slaves served the food and cleared the table. They also brought water for washing hands.
24110.m: Slaves served the guests at a banquet.

24111.q: What did a Roman banquet often start with?
24111.e: The starter was often eggs, olives or salad. At the end there was often fruit.
24111.m: A Roman banquet often began with eggs.

24112.q: What did Roman children often write on at school?
24112.e: A wax tablet was a wooden board with a thin layer of wax. You could write on it and rub it out again.
24112.m: Roman schoolchildren wrote on wax tablets.

24113.q: What did you write with on a wax tablet?
24113.e: The stylus was a pointed stick made of metal, bone or wood. It was used to scratch the letters into the wax.
24113.m: You wrote on a wax tablet with a stylus.

24114.q: What was the flat end of the stylus for?
24114.e: The flat end was used to smooth the wax again. This made the writing disappear.
24114.m: The flat end of the stylus rubbed out the writing.

24115.q: What was the frame of a wax tablet usually made of?
24115.e: The tablets were made of wood. The wax was spread into a hollow in the wood.
